#9617. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9614. Musée du Louvre, Musée d’Orsay and other Paris institutions to close on Saturday due to protests

Students from the École du Louvre blocked access to Musée du Louvre on 19 October to express their suppor" for the high school students' movement and to denounce "police repression"

Following scenes of looting and vandalism in several French cities, from Lyon to Limoges , on the sidelines of last weekend’s protests over the cost of living and in support of high school students, there is considerable apprehension on the eve of new demonstrations planned for this Saturday, 24 October. Curfews and bans on demonstrations are multiplying throughout France. In Paris, a march, the route of which has been approved by the police prefecture, will depart from the Place de la Bastille and proceed to the Place de la Nation. The government, overwhelmed by the violence of 17 October and heavily criticised since, has announced a reinforced security deployment.

In this highly tense context, shopkeepers are not the only ones to “close their doors”, or even barricade themselves in. Following the announcement of the early closure of the 2026 edition of the Art Basel Paris fair at the Grand Palais starting this Friday evening, several museums will remain closed this Saturday during the protests, for fear of further unrest.

The ministry of culture has announced the exceptional closure, as a security measure, of the Musée du Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Orangerie, and the Picasso National Museum in Paris. In coordination with the Paris Police Prefecture, the ministry “has asked all institutions under its supervision to implement all necessary measures to ensure the safety of visitors, the protection of staff, and the preservation of artworks,” according to a press release.

On the Paris Musées side, the Carnavalet Museum, the Maison de Victor Hugo, the Cognacq-Jay Museum and the Petit Palais will be closed.

The Louis Vuitton Foundation, currently exhibiting the Gustave Fayet collection, has also announced its precautionary closure, as have the Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection and the Cartier Foundation (all weekend). Many Parisian galleries will do the same this Saturday, including Poggi, Christian Berst – Art Brut, Magnin-A , Gagosian, and Hauser & Wirth.

Museums and cultural venues in the region are also taking precautions. It is advisable to check before visiting.

Italian officials say cultural institutions can open to the public so long as they ensure “visitors respect a distance of at least a metre between each other”

While Paris museum undergoes renovations, Europe's biggest modern and contemporary art collection will go on tour—keeping curators employed

The museum, located on the DePaul University campus, has been closed to the public since June

#9613. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9612. Mapping the ADHD Brain: How Neurotransmitters and Medication Work

The unique structures, wiring, and functionality of neurodivergent brains, according to science.

Why do one person’s ADHD symptoms differ from another’s? The answer lurks inside the structural and chemical differences of the ADHD brain.

No single brain region is the source of ADHD. However, subtle variations in brain structure, function, connectivity, and neurochemistry shape the neural networks that govern attention, motivation, reward, emotion, and self-control.

The regions involved in ADHD traits include:

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

The brain comprises billions of nerve cells called neurons. These neurons work in circuits, passing signals to each other that allow our bodies to think, move, remember, manage emotions, and control impulses.

Between neurons is a tiny gap called a synapse. To get messages across, neurons release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters into the gap. The neurotransmitters cross the gap and attach to receptors on the next neuron to help the message continue. Afterward, the brain clears neurotransmitters away in a process called reuptake.

The neurotransmitters dopamine (DE) and norepinephrine (NE) help the PFC hold goals and instructions in mind, filter distractions, and guide behavior. They also help reward circuits decide what feels interesting, urgent, or worth doing.

In ADHD, these signals don’t support those circuits and processes as strongly or consistently as they should. Task-relevant information may fade too quickly, while distractions, impulses, emotions or immediate rewards may pull more strongly. This is why ADHD is sometimes described as a “signal-to-noise” problem: the useful signal is there, but it may be drowned out by competing noise.

ADHD is linked to differences in how brain networks communicate and coordinate attention, motivation, emotion, and self-regulation.

ADHD medication can optimize brain signals by slowing the reuptake of DE or NE, increasing their release, or activating receptors that strengthen signaling. All of this helps guide attention, motivation, and self-control.

COMPARING THE IMPACTS OF ADHD MEDICATIONS

New insights: Functional connectivity data show that stimulants enhance performance by increasing vigilance and perceived task value.11 In other words, stimulants help the ADHD brain stay motivated and engaged with non-preferred tasks.

In addition to dopamine and norepinephrine, a third critical neurotransmitter is serotonin, which helps to regulate mood and emotion, both deeply relevant to the ADHD experience.

Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, and many people with the condition also live with mood disorders. Almost half of adults with ADHD are also prescribed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) – medications that increase serotonin levels to regulate mood, emotion, and sleep.

Viloxazine, a non-stimulant, became the first ADHD medication in the U.S. to also modulate serotonin. Beyond targeting ADHD symptoms, the medication was shown to improve co-occurring depression and anxiety in adults with all three conditions.12

Centanafadine (Simtriyo), a stimulant ADHD medication recently approved for children aged 6 years and older and adults, is a norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin reuptake inhibitor (NDSRI). Trials show that the medication improves symptoms in both groups and in adults with ADHD and co-occurring anxiety.13

Untreated ADHD impacts neural connectivity.14 Unstable brain connections increase risk for the development of anxiety, depression, insomnia, emotional frustration, and other challenges. ADHD medication enhances neural connectivity, but there are other ways to promote neural growth, protect the brain, and decrease risk for secondary issues.

Greg W. Mattingly, M.D., is an associate clinical professor at Washington University School of Medicine.

#9606. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

Many of the factors known to contribute to burnout are systemic and need to be addressed by health care organizations.2 However, physicians can take action to limit their stress and prevent exhaustion. The following strategies may help mitigate burnout2,4,13:

#9605. 3 Ways to Extinguish Emotional Reactivity

Smoldering flames may reignite. Rather than burying your emotions, try these strategies to minimize and outsmart them.

It starts with a spark — a critical comment, a goal unrealized — and our emotions quickly catch fire. This blaze can be public and palpable, or private and hidden. Spiraling thoughts, avoidance, self-criticism, and other reactive patterns may create a temporary sense of control, but they backfire over time, trapping us in reactivity loops that increase rather than reduce distress. They can also paralyze us.

When distressing emotions threaten to consume you, try the strategies below to neutralize or dampen them.

Observation, or mindful attention, is a foundational skill for emotional regulation because it creates a pause between stimulus and response.

To build this skill, alternate between focusing on your breath and on how your emotions live in your body – rapid heartbeat, knots in your stomach, tight fists, etc. Then expand your focus: What sights and sounds near and far do you notice? Now bring your attention back to your breath.

Fight the impulse to stuff down your emotions, as unpleasant or distressing as they may feel. For helpful cues, try saying “allow” aloud or picturing a green light through which your emotions can pass.

[Read: 7 Truths About ADHD and Intense Emotions]

Try these visual exercises to buy yourself even more time to process emotions. Imagine…

[Read: Why We Feel So Much — and Ways to Overcome It]

Shifting how you view a situation can modify your emotional response to it. Keep these reframing statements somewhere close and read them in moments of distress:

Over time, these skills will help you gain emotional clarity and choose actions that align with your values, not your reactive urges. In practice, that might mean taking a risk despite anxiety, putting the phone down instead of sending an angry text, forcing yourself to take a walk instead of isolating, or delaying gratification.

Douglas Mennin, Ph.D., is a professor of clinical psychology at Teachers College, Columbia University, in New York City.

#9600. As riots scar Paris’s luxury storefronts, Maison Guerlain opens art exhibition on Champs Elysées

Installation view of L’Heure des Possibles at Maison Guerlain in Paris

On Tuesday 20 October in Paris, among all the luxury boutiques on the avenue Champs-Elysées bearing the scars and graffiti sprayed on shopfronts by rioters just days before, Maison Guerlain opened L’Heure des Possibles, an exhibition of works by 33 artists.

The pieces, four of which were specially commissioned and the rest loaned, were sourced in response to one of Guerlain’s signature perfumes, L’Heure Bleue, and the period of twilight the fragrance takes its name from.

Wall-based works by well-known names including James Turrell, Annette Messager, Christian Boltanski and Ugo Rondinone have been installed throughout the historic maison alongside up-and-coming contemporary artists such as Marie Bovo, Xie Lei and Valentin Fougeray.

First founded in 1828 by Pierre-François-Pascal Guerlain, the Guerlain family built their hôtel particulier on the site in 1914.

“We need a moment of blue after all the black,” says Guerlain’s director of art, culture and heritage, Ann-Carolin Prazan, regarding the demonstrations that protested the state of education and cost-of-living in France, and which have been overshadowed by violent outbreaks by some ultra far-left groups. A VIP evening event marking the opening of the exhibition on 20 October at Maison Guerlain was cancelled.

“Paris is the capital of culture,” Prazan adds. “People want to support artists and culture; we must not be felled. I think we have to say ‘enough!’ now.”

Installation view of L’Heure des Possibles at Maison Guerlain in Paris

Despite President Emmanuel Macron saying “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days, France is bracing for another round of rioting this weekend, with Art Basel in Paris announcing yesterday that it is closing two days early as a safety precaution (Guerlain is a host partner of Art Basel Paris). Steps have already been taken to remove and protect some of the public sculptures that are dotted around the French capital as part of the Art Basel public programme.

Maison Guerlain, however, will remain open all weekend, according to a spokesman.

The perfume designer has an almost 200-year history of collaborating with artists from Matisse to Yves Klein and Lee Ufan. Its famous Bee Bottle, created in 1853 as a wedding present to Empress Eugenie de Montijo with Napoléon III, has been reinvented by contemporary and street artists including JonOne, Wassim Mraihi and Géraldine Gonzalez.

The company now has a vast archive of 25,000 works in its warehouse, many of them perfume bottle designs.

For the past 20 years, Guerlain has also held contemporary art exhibitions in the flagship boutique—a programme that has supported contemporary artists. The Paris-based artist Alexandra Mocanu, who has collaborated on an intricately embroidered work with the Swiss creative studio Retinaa, says Guerlain’s support has been “crucial” while she looks for a gallery in the French capital.

Prazan says she was unsure when she first started installing Modern and contemporary art in the maison in 2006. “It’s hardly a white cube,” she points out. “But it works.”

Unlike other luxury brands, Guerlain has remained streamlined in the products it makes, sticking to fragrances, skin care and makeup. This is perhaps unsurprising, given that the company was bought out in 1994 by LVMH, the world’s largest luxury goods conglomerate which manages more than 75 brands and made more than €80.8bn in revenue in 2025. Bernard Arnault, who owns LVMH, is one of France’s biggest art collectors, though the Guerlain collection remains a distinct entity.

The focus is now on the 200th anniversary of Guerlain in 2028, when a global exhibition featuring 20 artists is due to take place in Korea, Dubai, the US, China and Japan, among other places. “It’s going to be big, and it’s going to be totally unique,” Prazan says.

For its 30th anniversary, the Musée d’art moderne et contemporain invited the artist to show his monumental sculpture The Big Wave as part of a major retrospective

#9599. Study: Narcolepsy Medication Found to Improve Adult ADHD Symptoms

The orexin 2 receptor agonist called ALKS 7290 parallels stimulants’ path as a narcolepsy medication that evolved into an ADHD treatment.

An investigational narcolepsy medication called ALKS 7290, an orexin 2 receptor (OX2R) agonist, offers a new therapeutic approach for ADHD, according to results from a recent Phase 1B proof-of-concept study. ALKS 7290 is the first OX2R agonist to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms in adults with the condition, according to the drug’s manufacturer Alkermes plc.1

“OX2R agonists will represent an entirely new class of ADHD treatment, breaking the traditional barrier between stimulants and non-stimulant treatment,” says Greg Mattingly, M.D., a consultant on the Phase 1 and upcoming Phase 2 trials.

Stimulants remain a first-line treatment for ADHD in adults. However, not all patients tolerate the side effects of or see benefits from stimulant medications. According to an ADDitude survey of more than 11,000 adults with ADHD, 78% of respondents taking amphetamines and 70% of those taking methylphenidate experienced some side effects, compared to 66% of adults taking non-stimulant medications.

The drug works by selectively binding to and activating orexin type 2 receptors, proteins in the brain that regulate alertness, arousal, and appetite. This targeted approach could minimize potential side effects and drug misuse, according to Mattingly.

“Unlike traditional stimulants, orexin 2 receptor agonists have no direct effect on dopamine reuptake or release,” says Mattingly, Associate Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the Washington University School of Medicine. “Orexin 2 receptor agonists modulate pathways in the brain that are associated with vigilance, reward, and alertness while decreasing impulsivity. By minimizing direct effects on dopamine reuptake or release, they are considered to have a lower abuse potential.”

The two-week double-blind, parallel-group trial included 50 adults with ADHD and 88 adults without. Participants with ADHD were randomly assigned to receive ALKS 7290 at a total daily dose of 20 mg or 50 mg in split doses or placebo.

As early as day six, patients taking ALKS 7290 demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms, as measured by the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS), and in overall ADHD severity, as measured on the Clinical Global Impression-Severity Scale (CGI-S).

By day 14, treatment with ALKS 7290 reduced median baseline AISRS total scores by 14 points for the 20 mg dose and 19 points for the 50 mg dose. Median CGI-S scores declined by one point with the 20-mg dose and two points with the 50-mg dose.

ALKS 7290 was generally well tolerated at both doses, with mild side effects including insomnia, dizziness, change in sustained attention, and constipation.

The ORX2 agonist also shows promise in treating narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), a common co-occurring condition with ADHD. (Approximately 25% of people with narcolepsy have ADHD.).2 In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Orzeyful (oveporexton), a first-in-class OX2R agonist tablet indicated to treat narcolepsy type l (NT1) in adults.3 Takeda Pharmaceuticals, Orzeyful’s manufacturer, expects the drug to be available in November 2026, pending DEA scheduling.

NT1 is a chronic sleep disorder, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy, and sleep disruptions, resulting from a deficiency in orexin-producing neurons.4

ADHD and narcolepsy share several overlapping symptoms related to arousal and wakefulness. Before becoming standard ADHD treatment, stimulants like amphetamine and methylphenidate were used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness found in narcolepsy patients.5

“Our longest surveillance of the safety of amphetamine comes from following people with narcolepsy for their entire lives,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. Today, Ritalin (methylphenidate) and Adderall (amphetamine) are both central nervous system stimulant medications approved for the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy in adults and children.

While it is too soon to know if the OX2R agonist used to treat narcolepsy will likewise evolve into a standard ADHD treatment, the parallels to stimulant medications are clear.

“What’s exciting for clinicians was the fact that ALKS 7290 had dose-related improvement in ADHD symptoms with dramatic improvement seen early and sustained throughout the two-week study,” says Mattingly, founding partner of St. Charles Psychiatric Associates. “While preliminary, the level of improvement obtained with this molecule after two weeks was similar to what is typically seen after four to six weeks in a trial of methylphenidate or amphetamine molecules for ADHD treatment.”

Results from a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of ALKS 7290 in adults with ADHD are expected in 2027.

#9597. ADHD Lacks a Biomarker Test… But Not Scientific Validity

ADHD’s validity is confirmed not by a blood test but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence, including a reliable behavioral phenotype, genetic heritability, measurable life impairments, and more.

The diagnostic legitimacy of ADHD has been vigorously debated in contemporary psychiatry circles. For parents navigating a child’s diagnosis or adults receiving a later-in-life diagnosis, the central paradox is this: ADHD has profound, life-altering symptoms but no definitive biological test, such as a blood panel or a brain scan, to confirm its presence.

This absence of biomarkers is frequently cited by critics who characterize ADHD as a modern social construct, a byproduct of high-pressure academic environments, or a medicalization of normal childhood energy. However, the scientific consensus, codified in the 2021 World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statements, asserts that ADHD is a valid, highly heritable, and neurobiologically grounded disorder.1

In modern medicine, the gold standard for disease validation is a typically quantifiable, objective indicator of a biological state. When you are sick or injured, you expect a physician to draw blood, perform a biopsy, or order a scan or some other laboratory test. Because this reliance on objective evidence is so deeply ingrained, skeptics and critics of ADHD point to the absence of a definitive biomarker as evidence of its illegitimacy. However, these critics misunderstand (or intentionally ignore) this well-known fact: Many indisputably valid disorders cannot be affirmed with biomarker tests.

In fact, painful and disabling disorders such as migraine headaches, trigeminal neuralgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis, complex regional pain syndrome, interstitial cystitis, and mild traumatic brain injury are indisputably physical, nonpsychiatric medical diseases without biomarkers. What these critics ignore is that most, if not all, nonpsychiatric medical disorders were viewed as disorders long before a biomarker test was available.

Medical science says that we observe suffering, seek to understand its causes and treatments, and ideally, find a biomarker for diagnosis. But in the absence of a biomarker, we still must help those in need.

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

Critics of ADHD as a diagnosis also ignore the fact that psychiatric science has established criteria for what is, and what is not, a disorder. In a 2005 paper, “The Scientific Foundation for Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder as a Valid Psychiatric Disorder,” I documented how ADHD meets all these criteria.2 Below is a summary.

Does ADHD have a consistent and recognizable pattern of symptoms and functional impairments? Yes. Inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity are well defined, and those with ADHD have clear functional impairments, ranging from severe academic problems and poor peer relations to accidental injuries and occupational failure. A trait becomes a disorder when it is associated with significant distress or disability, and most people with ADHD would agree that their condition brings both.

Does ADHD have objective correlates, such as neuroimaging, psychological testing, or biochemical markers? Indeed, many studies have documented impaired performance on neuropsychological tests, small differences in brain structure and function, and genetic variants that increase risk for ADHD. This criterion does not require the correlates to be useful for diagnosis, only that they are more likely to be observed in those with the condition compared to those without.

Though individuals with ADHD are at higher risk for other disorders, the symptoms used to diagnose ADHD are different from those used to diagnose commonly coexisting disorders such as anxiety and mood disorders.

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

Does ADHD have a trajectory across the lifespan? Yes, the continuation of symptoms from childhood to adulthood and the emergence of other disorders associated with ADHD have been well documented.

Is there evidence of a genetic cause for ADHD? Yes, ADHD has high heritability and DNA studies show that most cases of ADHD are caused by the accumulation of many genetic risk variants.

Does ADHD have a predictable and beneficial response to specific therapeutic interventions? Yes, substantial evidence supports the benefit of stimulant and non-stimulant medications as well as parent behavior therapy for children and cognitive behavioral therapy for adults.

ADHD’s existence is undeniable. The application of these criteria to ADHD provides a rigorous scientific defense against the claim that the disorder is merely a collection of subjective labels. Its validity is established, not by a simple lab or blood test, but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence: a highly reliable behavioral phenotype, strong genetic heritability, distinct population-level neurobiological correlates, severe and measurable life impairments, and a clear response to medical and psychological treatments. Waiting for a perfect biomarker while children and adults suffer preventable harms would abandon medical responsibility.

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., is a distinguished professor of psychiatry at SUNY Upstate Medical University. He is the founder of the ADHDEvidenceProject.org.

#9596. Struggling with impulse control? Try these 7 tips

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You send the text before you finish thinking it through. You put in an online order before asking yourself whether you really need it. You eat three bites of the snack before you realize you’re not even hungry.

Impulsive moments like these aren't signs of a character flaw. They reflect your brain's tendency to act before it fully evaluates the consequences. For some people, that tendency shows up during a stressful stretch and eases once life calms down. For others, especially those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), it's more of a constant struggle. Either way, impulse control is a skill you can improve.

So, what does this mean for you? Let’s break down what drives impulse control, and what you can do about it.

Impulse control is your ability to pause before you act on an urge, thought, or emotion — that split second where you decide whether to follow through.

Your prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain responsible for planning and thinking ahead, mostly handles this. When it's working well, it helps catch an impulse before that impulse becomes an action.

If your impulse control feels shaky at times, that’s not necessarily a willpower problem. It usually means your brain is under strain from stress, poor sleep, or emotional overload.

Most people who act impulsively on occasion don’t have a diagnosed disorder. For others, though, struggling to resist harmful urges is a persistent pattern. Impulse control disorder covers conditions like intermittent explosive disorder (sudden, disproportionate anger), kleptomania (compulsive stealing), pyromania (compulsive fire-setting), and compulsive gambling. These conditions may respond well to professional support, such as therapy or medication.

Your brain relies on two systems that don't always agree. The limbic system reacts fast, driven by emotion and instinct. The prefrontal cortex works slower, weighing your options before you act.

When you're calm and rested, the prefrontal cortex can keep impulsive urges in check. When your brain is pushed past its capacity, the limbic system takes over instead. Impulse control shifts throughout the day depending on how you're feeling, which is why the same urge can feel manageable to sit with one moment and impossible to resist the next.

A few factors can make impulse control harder:

sleep deprivation, which weakens your brain's ability to regulate behavior

chronic stress, which keeps your brain in a heightened, reactive state

strong emotions that feel too intense to ignore or resist

substance use, which affects your brain's decision-making centers

ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions, where pausing may be a challenge throughout daily life, not just under pressure

Like any skill, impulse control strengthens with practice. The tips below work at different layers: some help in the moment, while others ease the mental strain that makes urges harder to resist in the first place. Feel free to start with one or two that feel relevant to you.

Impulsive urges can feel pressing, but they don’t have to dictate what you do next. Often, just pausing for a moment is enough to break the pull.

Try: Counting to ten, taking a slow breath, or naming what you're feeling out loud. Some people find a go-to phrase useful, such as "not yet" or "wait and see" to delay their response. Over time, this habit starts to feel more natural.

💙 Learn how to Resist Emotional Urges with Dr. Julie Smith on Calm.

Most impulsive behavior follows a pattern. It tends to spike around conflict, boredom, overwhelm, hunger, or fatigue. Once you learn your triggers, you can work with them instead of reacting in the moment.

Try: Keeping a brief log for a week or two. Note when impulsivity shows up, what leads to it, and how you feel. Once you spot a pattern—say, you're most reactive before meals or after a difficult conversation—you can plan around it.

Eat before that difficult conversation. Save demanding tasks for your sharper hours. Take a breath before responding to messages that tend to trigger a reaction.

💙 Discover Dr. Judson Brewer’s Breaking Bad Habits masterclass on Calm.

Under pressure, your brain defaults to what's fast and familiar. If-then planning gives it a prepared response instead, so you're not improvising when emotions are running high.

Try: "If [situation], then I'll [response]." For example, "If I feel the urge to reply right away, then I'll wait 10 minutes first." Or "If I'm about to make an unplanned purchase, then I'll add it to a list and revisit it in 48 hours." The more specific the plan, the harder it is to talk yourself out of it later.

💙 Walk through this process with Calm’s If-Then session with Jay Shetty.

Impulse control runs on limited fuel: sleep, stress, and mental bandwidth all shape how much of it you have on a given day. That's why impulsive urges tend to show up most at the end of a long day or after a stretch of bad sleep.

You can't eliminate every source of strain, but you can cut down on low-stakes daily decisions. Try prepping meals or laying out clothes the night before — that way, you're not making choices when you're already running on empty.

It’s also worth protecting what restores you, including sleep, movement, time away from screens, and nourishing meals.

Struggling with too many decisions? Here are 8 tips for when your mental energy is low.

Regular mindfulness practice builds your ability to pause as an ongoing habit, not just in the moment an impulse hits. Start with a few minutes a day, and keep at it on a schedule that works for you.

Try: Focusing on your breathing during practice. When you notice an urge come up (to shift position, check your phone, stop early), gently return your attention to your breath instead of acting on it.

💙 Start with the Basics of Mindfulness from the 7 Days of Calm series.

New habits can be tempting to abandon in the moment. Outside structure, like asking someone to check in on you, gives you accountability beyond your own willpower.

Try: Telling someone about the pattern you're trying to change. Even saying it out loud can make it harder to slide back into old habits.

If you’d rather handle this on your own, here are 6 ways to hold yourself accountable.

If your impulsivity is a constant pattern that impacts your relationships, work, and daily life, self-directed strategies may not be enough.

A therapist trained in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help you identify what's driving your behavior and develop more effective responses. If ADHD is part of the picture, an assessment can open the door to options like medication.

If you're not sure where to start, your primary care provider is a good first stop.

Poor impulse control can look like interrupting people mid-conversation, buying things without thinking it through, snapping in anger, or acting on cravings without a second thought. It tends to show up most when you're under pressure, drained, or emotionally overwhelmed.

If you have ADHD, tools such as if-then planning give your brain a prepared response before the moment of temptation arrives. Consistent mindfulness practice can also help you build the capacity to pause in those moments.

If impulsivity is getting in the way of your work, relationships, or daily life, it's worth talking to your doctor or an ADHD specialist. For some people, medication can meaningfully help.

Impulse control disorder may involve anger that feels bigger than the situation calls for, compulsive stealing, or gambling that's negatively impacting your life. If resisting an urge feels out of your control, that's worth bringing to a doctor — this condition is treatable.

Stress puts your brain into threat-response mode, which interferes with the part of your brain that handles careful decisions. That heightened stress state is useful in an actual emergency, where speed is more important than reflection. But in everyday situations, it makes thoughtful decision-making harder.

Mindfulness trains the same skill impulse control relies on: noticing an urge without immediately acting on it. Regular practice improves attention and emotional regulation, which makes it easier to find that pause in tempting situations. This can be especially useful if you have ADHD or you’re working on substance-related impulsivity.

Check out how a regular mindfulness practice can support your overall mental well-being.

The amount of time it takes to improve impulse control depends on your situation and your approach. Tools such as if-then planning or pausing before big decisions can help within a few weeks, while mindfulness and therapy tend to take longer — often several months of consistent practice.

Self-control is broader than impulse control: it covers habits like managing emotions and staying on task. Impulse control is more specific: it's about what you do in the gap between having an urge and acting on it. You can have strong self-control overall and still struggle with impulses in the moment, or be quick to pause in the moment while your broader self-control could use work.

#9595. Students stage protest performance over closure of Chicago's DePaul Art Museum

The Waiting protest outside the DePaul Art Museum in Chicago on 8 October Photo: Ruth Lopez

The closure in June of DePaul University’s esteemed DePaul Art Museum (DPAM) has rankled the arts community in Chicago. Students returning to campus this autumn responded to that loss with a communal piece of public protest art titled Waiting.

The format was simple: at 5pm on 8 October, a queue began to form at the front door of the shuttered museum. For the next hour, more than 100 people stood solemnly in the line stretching far down the sidewalk.

“The art department feels underfunded and forgotten by the administration,” said Ursula DeBray, a 22-year-old art student from Washington state. “Closing the museum felt like DePaul took ten steps backwards.”

This sentiment was shared by others who came to the protest hoping to convince the university's leadership to reconsider its decision to close the museum. “It’s showing that there was a community that got impacted by funding decisions,” said art student Jaret Ledford.

The DPAM had provided a cultural refuge for the campus community and surrounding neighbourhood of Lincoln Park, including educational and work-study opportunities. While the museum’s doors are now closed to the public, it remains minimally staffed to accommodate class visits and meet its obligation to a funded fellowship in museum studies.

The school responded to the protest the following day, saying in a statement: “DePaul University welcomes this peaceful demonstration in support of the arts in Chicago. The decision to stop operations at the DePaul Art Museum was a difficult one, as many institutions around the country are facing budgetary constraints. The arts are a critical part of DePaul’s community and academic offerings, and the university has no plans to sell the art collection or the building.”

The statement went on to say that university leadership was working with a faculty task force “to guide the next chapter of this space and collection” and expects to receive a report with recommendations from the group in December.

Most of the artists, students and faculty at the protest expressed frustration with the university’s partiality to sports. Just days before, the university had celebrated the groundbreaking for a $42m sports complex after demolishing four 1890s rowhouses. The building site is just around the corner from the museum, making the disparate spending decisions impossible to ignore.

“I don’t quite understand some of the funding priorities of academic institutions,” said Dana Boutin, an independent researcher and curator who held a handmade “I ❤️ DPAM” sign.

Boutin pointed out that another local college, the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC), recently sold the 19th-century home that once housed the Roger Brown Study Collection. Brown’s home and studio had been given to SAIC by the eponymous painter and collector in 1996, but its contents were later donated to the Wisconsin-based Art Preserve. Although the objects and art ended up in a more simpatico institution, SAIC had succeeded in dismantling a historic and culturally important experience for its art-school community.

“These are laboratories for students to learn and get professional experience,” Boutin said.

The mood in the queue at DPAM was wistful. Maybe it had something to do with the fact that the lights were still on in the museum, and that its collection will not be dispersed. DPAM’s director, Laura-Caroline de Lara, remains at the museum as the steward of its 4,000-piece collection. She said she has received many requests for external loans and is now in conversation with the Art Bridges Foundation about entering its collection-sharing programme.

The Fondation Louis Vuitton, the Musée National Picasso‑Paris and the Maison de Victor Hugo are also shutting their doors as a precautionary measure

The fate of the 4,000 objects—including works by Christina Ramberg, Roger Brown, Martin Puryear and Edra Soto—remains unclear

The sprawling new campus on Chicago's South Side includes a rousing museum and commissions by Mark Bradford, Maya Lin, Richard Hunt, Martin Puryear and many more

New exhibition is dedicated to Margaret Demant—a passionate booster of the Detroit Institute of Arts’ collection

#9594. Christmas traditions: 12 meaningful ways to celebrate

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Let’s be real — Christmas comes with a lot of traditions. And by traditions, sometimes we mean — baggage. The holidays can be cozy and warm and filled with love. But they can also be overwhelming, exhausting, and sometimes kind of sad.

The expectations of the season can also add a ton of pressure. You’re supposed to have time to not only think of thoughtful presents, but also brave the scary, jam-packed stores to go and buy them. You’re supposed to make your grandma’s cherished holiday recipe (that just so happens to take half the day to make.) And you’re supposed to be happy and grateful the entire time — even when you receive lottery scratch cards from your Dad, when you gifted him a personalized luxury watch.

But rather than getting caught up in what Christmas is supposed to be or the baggage of what it has been in the past, maybe this year, you slow down, reset, and start creating traditions that do work for you and your chosen family.

Traditions don’t need to be stressful or perfect — they can be whatever you and yours want them to be. Here’s a list of twelve simple and fun traditions that hopefully will help bring you some warm, gooey feelings this holiday season. Let’s unwrap them!

In your family, it could be tradition to go to a Christmas tree farm, get really angry at each other because everyone thinks the other family members have zero “Christmas tree taste,” and then eventually you settle on one that is “fine” but will do for this year.

Then later, you all laugh at how heated you got and you look warmly at your newly decorated tree, thinking, “Wow, actually, this is my favorite Christmas tree yet. I can’t wait to fight with them all over again next year.”

There’s no tried and true formula for getting a tradition right. If it makes you and your loved ones feel good, laugh, and bond, then that’s what matters. Here are some ideas you could start with your family or chosen family this year that might accomplish just that.

Decking the halls isn’t just about making your home look red, and green, and festive all over — it’s a chance to make something pretty together as a team and make some memories in the process.

So blast fun holiday music, break out your favorite ornaments, and dance it out as you hang stockings, put up lights, and add whatever decorations means Christmas to you. Maybe make it a friendly competition like, “Who can place the ornaments on the tree before ‘Last Christmas’ ends?”

Tip: If you’re short on time or you’re only interested in decorating for an hour, keep it simple. Maybe just set up a small tree or decorate only the window that you’ll pass the most often.

Make it mindful: As you decorate, consider taking time to share memories of what some of the decorations make you remember from past holidays, and what you’re looking forward to for this upcoming holiday season.

A lot of the holiday season feels like it’s about “doing” something. It’s easy to feel like you’re always running around or making something. Watching a Christmas classic can be a great, low key way to get some quality time, unwind, and bond. So go snuggle up under some cozy blankets with your loved ones, sip on some hot cocoa, and much on peppermint bark as you watch your favorite holiday classic.

Tip: If you can’t decide on “A Christmas Story” or “Elf” or “Home Alone” and it’s getting heated, maybe do a movie marathon schedule for the week and let everyone get a chance to pick their favorite film.

Make it mindful: Before pressing play, put away your phones and be fully present in the movie. Notice the feelings of being cozy on the couch, and enjoy the sounds of the familiar soundtrack or the laughter of your favorite people. (And maybe wait ‘til after the movie to google what else James Caan was in besides “Elf.”)

Add some personality to your tree and design homemade ornaments together. Bust out paints, markers, glitter etc. and make each other bust out laughing at your (potentially terrible) homemade designs. A perfectly decorated tree can be boring, but one that has your best friend’s accidental three-eyed Santa might be just the thing to always make you smile.

Tip: If crafting just makes you think of the hours of cleanup after, try writing cute little notes about the past year and tucking them inside clear ornaments instead.

Make it mindful: Focus on the process rather than the end result while you're crafting. Enjoy the textures, sounds, and feelings of working with your hands. And don’t forget to marvel at your friends and family’s creativity, or attempt at creativity.

💙 Pop on the Wintertime Piano playlist for a cozy take on some holiday classics while you get your craft on.

In a perfect world, we’re volunteering and giving back all the time. But life tends to get in the way. Don’t beat yourself up for not volunteering more though. Instead maybe use the holidays as an excuse to not only bond with your loved ones but to also commit to doing one sweet act of giving back together.

It doesn’t need to be big like volunteering at a food bank (though that would be a great one!). It can be something small like everyone meeting at a local charity spot and donating one toy or book they no longer use.

Tip: Choose a smaller activity that fits your family and friend’s schedule and abilities to make it easier for everyone to follow through.

Make it mindful: After volunteering, ask everyone how it made them feel and maybe share some love for all that you have to be grateful for.

Every year, we see kids excitedly write letters to Santa. But why can’t we also join in on that fun? Maybe this year, you and your loved ones have a letter writing party to Santa, or to each other. Writing letters can be a good way to share what you love about one another, express gratitude, and talk about your hopes for the coming year. You can even wait to read them until Christmas Eve or Christmas morning and turn the letters into a fun gift opening moment.

Tip: If you do have little ones who want to write to Santa, make it extra fun by “mailing” the letters in a decorated box.

Make it mindful: While writing the letters, encourage everyone to focus on gratitude and specific warm and fuzzy memories in their letters. Here are eight more gratitude exercises you could practice throughout the holiday season.

There’s a reason caroling has been around for so long. It’s fun and a great way to spread holiday cheer. But if singing door-to-door sounds terrifying to you, don’t stress. Instead, maybe host a family and friends karaoke night at home with a playlist of your fave holiday hits.

Tip: If singing in public sounds like a nightmare, but you do enjoy singing privately or with loved ones, maybe try something small and do a one song sing-along around your own Christmas tree as you decorate the tree.

Make it mindful: Before singing, set an intention, like spreading happiness or wanting to be silly. Focus on the joy it brings you, not the quality of your performance.

Tip: After you’ve done a thorough “taste test” of all the baked goods, consider packaging up the extra treats and giving them away to your neighbors, co-workers, and teachers.

Make it mindful: Slow down and savor the process. Notice the smells, textures, and flavors as you bake. These eight tips can help you practice some mindful cooking.

If you’re looking for a break from technology or the stress of the holiday season, reading can be a great way to quiet the mind and create a sense of calm for you and your friends and family. Hosting a cozy story night might be a simple but meaningful way to slow down and enjoy the season with your loved ones. You could pick a chapter or two from your favorite holiday book and read it aloud together while drinking peppermint tea.

Tip: If you’d rather give your eyes a rest, consider listening to a chapter from a Christmas themed audiobook or a Sleep Story.

Make it mindful: While listening, visualize the story and give yourself over fully to the experience without distractions.

💙 Have the whole family jump aboard The Christmas Express for a magical train ride through the heart of Christmas in this cozy Sleep Story.

Somehow December always gets here and we think, how’s it already the end of the year? It was January ten minutes ago. Rather than getting sad at how much time has passed though, use it as an opportunity to celebrate the highlights of the year. Host a scrapbook making night with your family and friends and have everyone fill it with their favorite photos, ticket stubs, and other meaningful keepsakes.

It can become something you and your loved ones can add to every year and it gives you something tangible to look back on as a family.

Tip: If scrapbooking feels like way too much time and energy, maybe create a digital photo album or slideshow instead.

Make it mindful: As you look through your memories, take time to really take it in and feel grateful for all the wonderful experiences you and your loved ones have had this year.

We all dream of days where we can sit and literally do nothing, except be with friends and family. The holidays can be a perfect time to finally make this dream a reality. Pick a day and invite your loved ones over to cook a big breakfast, play games, watch movies, and just relax in sweats or pajamas.

Tip: If cooking is too much, dive into those leftovers or treat yourself – order takeout.

Make it mindful: Make this a screen-free day. Focus on staying present and savoring the little moments (here are nine tips to help), like laughing over how many blankets your sibling is currently wearing.

It’s nice to have a little something to look forward to every day. With your nearest and dearest, consider having a night where everyone comes over to make their own advent calendar filled with activities you could do together instead of treats. You might write down simple ideas like “make hot chocolate,” or “hide the pickle ornament in the tree.” Then each day, open a new card and do the activity together.

Tip: If you’re short on time, plan quick and easy activities like, “Everyone go hang up your stocking on the fireplace.”

Make it mindful: After each activity, pause and reflect on the joy of doing something small and fun together.

Sometimes we’re too busy to take in the sheer magic of the season and all of its decorations. Maybe make a night with your loved ones to drive through a local light show or walk around a decorated neighborhood. This can be a fun way to start an easy tradition where the only thing you have to do is take in all the beauty that’s around you.

Tip: Pack snacks and a thermos of hot chocolate!

Make it mindful: While exploring, take a moment to pause and soak in the sights.

💙 Learn how to Savor the Moment (and how it can benefit you) this holiday season with help from Jay Shetty.

Christmas traditions are customs that people repeat each year to mark the holiday. Some are common in many homes, like decorating a tree, giving gifts, singing carols, and sharing a meal. Others are personal to a family, like a yearly pajama day or a movie night with one agreed-upon classic. What makes a tradition meaningful is the time you spend together, and you can always start new ones.

A tradition can be whatever you want it to be. But easier traditions to follow through on tend to be ones that are simple, small and don’t require much time or effort. Some examples are:

Light a candle together: Every night in December, try taking turns lighting a candle and sharing one small thing that made you smile or laugh that day.

Sip a warm drink by the tree: Spend a few minutes each morning or evening standing by your Christmas tree and enjoying some hot cocoa or your favorite beverage.

Reminisce over Christmas dinner: Go around the table and bring up one memory from a past Christmas that meant something to you.

Traditions usually mean more when the emphasis is not on the activity itself but more so on the bonding time you shared with your loved ones. Focus on slowing down and savoring the moment as opposed to simply checking off a holiday task. These eight tips can help you take it all in.

If you’re baking with your family one night, take time to enjoy the scents, tastes, and laughter. Maybe add a gratitude jar and have everyone write down something they’re thankful for during the season.

Kids thrive on connection and routine, so simple traditions can be perfect for them. Small intentional activities help make them feel included. Some fun and easy examples you could try with kids are:

Sitting by the tree and reading them a short story

Making holiday crafts like ornaments with them

Drawing on construction paper together to make wrapping paper

Being away from home at Christmas can be really lonely and tough. But creating small rituals that anchor you in the moment, like lighting a candle, saying a quiet toast, or reflecting on what you’re grateful for can help to make it a little easier.

If you’re still missing family and friends, Facetime is a great way to stay in touch and still see your loved ones. Maybe even try opening presents or singing carols together.

Blending Christmas and Hanukkah is a fun way to celebrate connection across traditions — and maybe even get double the presents. If you’re in one of these families, focus on making moments that honor both.

You could write down one thing you’re thankful for each night of Hanukkah and then display those notes as ornaments on your Christmas tree. You could also light the menorah and read a Christmas story in the same evening.

This is a comprehensive table of psychiatry ICD 10 codes used by researchers and healthcare professionals and personnel – nurses, medical coders, physicians, et al. This table has been curated for psychiatrists and mental health specialists to include all psychiatry ICD 10 codes and classifications relevant to psychiatric and mental health conditions.

The World Health Organization originally authorized the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) for mortality coding and classification from United States death certificates. A Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) was developed for medical diagnoses, and a Procedure Coding System (ICD-10-PCS) was used to classify inpatient procedures. Psychiatry ICD-10 codes in the ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS replace and update psychiatry ICD codes in all three volumes of the ICD-9-CM.

#9592. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9591. Holiday anxiety: causes, symptoms, and 10 ways to cope

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We often think of the holiday season as a magical time filled with joy, family gatherings, and celebrations. And it can be. However, for many people, this time of year can also usher in a wave of holiday anxiety, a type of stress associated with the many demands and expectations of the festive season.

Holiday anxiety is a specific type of stress that occurs during holiday seasons. It's different from everyday stress, because it's linked to the unique pressures and expectations that come with holiday events and traditions. Understanding holiday anxiety and recognizing its effects on our mental health can help us manage it effectively. Here are some of the ways it can manifest:

Emotional overload: The holidays can bring a range of emotions, both happy and sad. For some, reminders of lost loved ones or past experiences can lead to feelings of grief or nostalgia.

Physical symptoms: Anxiety can cause physical symptoms like headaches, fatigue, or digestive problems. These can be exacerbated by holiday indulgences and disrupted routines.

Social stress: The pressure to socialize, host events, or interact with family members you might not see regularly can be overwhelming, especially if there are a lot of late nights involved. This is especially true for those with existing social anxieties.

Routine disruption: Regular routines are often disrupted during the holidays, which can be particularly challenging for those who find comfort and stability in their daily schedules.

Acknowledge your feelings around holiday anxiety and remember that it's okay to feel stressed or overwhelmed during the holiday season. Taking proactive steps to manage your mental health can help make the holidays a more enjoyable and less stressful time.

Increased stress levels: Additional demands in the holiday season can lead to heightened stress levels, impacting mental health.

Mood fluctuations: The highs and lows can cause mood swings, bouts of sadness, irritability, and even depression.

Sleep disruption: Anxiety can disturb sleep patterns, leading to insomnia or poor-quality sleep, which, in turn, affects overall wellbeing.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms: Some people might resort to habits like overeating, excessive drinking, or withdrawing from social interactions, which can further impact their mental health.

While what triggers one person may not trigger another, there are a few ways that holiday anxiety can manifest. Identifying your unique triggers can help you prepare tools and strategies to better handle anxiety during this busy season. While the holidays can be an important time, protecting your mental health is more important.

The media and social norms often portray the holidays as a time of perfection and endless joy. This can set unrealistic expectations for the ideal holiday experience, leading to disappointment and stress when reality doesn't match these ideals.

Holidays often come with financial burdens, including the cost of gifts, travel, decorations, and hosting events. Worrying about how to afford these expenses can cause significant stress.

Holidays often feature family gatherings, which can be challenging if relationships are strained or there's a history of conflict. Navigating these dynamics, especially in larger gatherings, can bring anxiety.

The holiday season is filled with invitations to social events, expectations to meet, and tasks to complete. Trying to do everything can lead to burnout and feeling overwhelmed.

For those who’ve lost loved ones or are far from family, the holidays can intensify feelings of grief or isolation. The contrast between personal experience and the general festivity can be overwhelming.

Comparing your own holiday experience to what others seem to be doing online or social media can lead to feelings of inadequacy and dissatisfaction.

Traveling during the holidays can be chaotic and stressful because of busy airports, traffic jams, and the fear of plans being disrupted or not going as scheduled.

The change in daily routines during the holidays, such as altered eating habits, sleep schedules, and exercise, can contribute to stress and anxiety.

Managing holiday anxiety effectively involves practical strategies that focus on self-care and mindfulness. These tips can help you navigate the holiday season with less stress, more enjoyment, and better mental health.

Make a list of holiday activities and rank them in order of importance to you. Focus on the top few that bring you the most joy or are the most meaningful. This can help reduce the feeling of being overwhelmed, ensuring you spend your time and energy on what truly matters to you.

Cut back on elaborate plans. Instead, go for simpler celebrations or low-key gatherings to reduce the pressure and expectations. Smaller, intimate gatherings often bring more joy than large, stressful events.

Enjoy holiday treats but avoid overeating by listening to your body's hunger and fullness cues. Mindful eating can help you maintain physical and mental wellbeing, as overindulgence can often lead to physical discomfort and emotional guilt.

💙 Explore Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Eating Practice and learn the fundamentals of mindfulness at mealtime and how it can help your overall stress and anxiety.

Remind yourself that it’s okay for things not to be perfect, and be realistic about what you can achieve and what the holidays can offer. Having realistic expectations can significantly reduce disappointment and stress.

💙 Learn to let go of what was supposed to be and embrace what is with Jay Shetty’s guided meditation on Expectations.

Don’t pack your schedule too tightly. Instead, plan for breaks and downtime in your holiday schedule. Rest is essential for helping you to recharge, and it allows opportunities for spontaneous activities, too.

💙 When it’s time for bed, make it count by listening to Oren Jay Sofer’s guided sleep meditation, Deep Rest.

Whenever you feel stressed, take a moment to focus on your breathing. Inhale deeply for a count of four, hold for a count of four, and exhale for a count of four to help calm the mind and reduce anxiety.

💙 Use your breath to calm your mind and anxiety in three minutes with Breathe to Calm Down.

Set a budget for holiday spending and stick to it. Consider homemade gifts or shared experiences instead of expensive purchases. This can help reduce holiday anxiety caused by financial strain.

💙 Set Financial Intentions and goals this holiday season, and stick to them.

Not everything will go as planned, so be open to accepting it, and find humor and joy in the imperfect moments. Embracing imperfection can lead to a more relaxed and enjoyable holiday experience.

💙 Shift your energy from perfectionism to going with the flow with this meditation on Energy Management to help guide you toward ease.

Reduce the time you spend on social media to avoid unhealthy comparisons. Limiting social media can help maintain a more realistic perspective and reduce feelings of inadequacy.

💙 Release yourself from the Social Mania comparison by forgoing social media during the holidays.

Reach out to supportive friends, family, or a professional if you feel the holiday stress is too much to handle alone. Talking about your feelings and sharing your experiences can provide relief and remind you you’re not alone in your feelings.

The holidays can be a source of anxiety due to a combination of high expectations, financial pressures, family dynamics, and the disruption of normal routines. The holidays are often portrayed as a time of complete joy and perfect family gatherings, but when reality doesn't match up, it can lead to feelings of inadequacy or disappointment. The holidays can also be a reminder of lost loved ones or past difficulties, contributing to feelings of sadness or loneliness for many people.

The 3-3-3 rule is a simple mindfulness technique to help ground yourself during anxious moments. This exercise can help bring your focus back to the present, interrupting the cycle of anxious thoughts.

Name three things you can see around you.

Move three parts of your body, like your ankle, fingers, and shoulder.

There are plenty of actionable ways to calm holiday anxiety.

Prioritize self-care activities like mindful breathing or a relaxing bath.

Engage in regular physical activity to help relieve stress.

Keep a regular sleep schedule to ensure adequate rest.

Set realistic expectations for the holidays.

Simplify plans and focus only on what matters most to you.

Seek support from friends, family, or professionals.

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed during Christmas. The holiday season can be a hectic time with lots of social obligations, financial pressures, and the emotional weight of personal or family expectations. It's important to recognize these feelings and take steps to manage them, like setting boundaries, asking for help when needed, and taking time for self-care.

To manage social anxiety during Thanksgiving, plan ahead for social interactions. Have some conversation topics ready to ease into interactions. Set boundaries for yourself, and step away for a moment if you feel overwhelmed. Focus on making connections with one or two people rather than trying to engage with everyone. Practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing before and during the event. And remember, it's okay to limit social gatherings to what feels manageable for you.

Yes. Anxiety can build before a trip, show up during it, or both, often from planning pressure or the work you left behind. If this is your main concern, our guide to vacation anxiety covers what to do before, during, and after your holiday.
