#9590. ADHD and the Social Processing Gap

“There’s a difference between having social skills and being able to use them consistently in the moment. This is the fundamental challenge for people living with ADHD.”

“Knowing social expectations versus implementing them in real time is a very big challenge for people with ADHD.” — Sharon Saline, Psy.D.

This tension is at the heart of many slip-ups — from oversharing and interrupting to difficulties reading the room — that stump adults with ADHD across various scenarios. Dr. Saline, a clinical psychologist who specializes in ADHD, described this as the “social processing gap” during her October ADDitude webinar, “Reading Body Language & Social Cues: A Primer for People with ADHD.”

Here, learn more about the gap and how to fill it, along with quick tips for navigating sticky social situations with ease and confidence.

ADHD symptoms and traits — like working memory challenges, distractibility, impulsivity, hyperfocus and more — directly impact communication and social skills. But there’s another factor that tends to influence social interactions: shame.

We asked: Which of the following social challenges prompted you to be here today — for yourself or someone important to you? (Select all that apply.)

A history of negative and uncomfortable social interactions means that many adults with ADHD approach social situations assuming they’ll misread a facial expression, take up too much of the conversation, or commit a faux pas. As a result, many are unable to fully participate in conversations without extreme vigilance and/or becoming overwhelmed, anxious, self-conscious, or exhausted.

“ADHD affects our ability to interpret social information when it’s occurring in real time, because of anxiety and rejection sensitivity that complicate those interpretations and how people respond,” Saline said.

Navigating misunderstandings in relationships, friendships, family, and work comes down to three words: Notice. Check. Clarify.

Noticing, or building social awareness, doesn’t mean scanning for signs of disapproval. It is being attuned to other people and adapting to connection, without taking things too personally or making assumptions. “The challenge is to notice these cues without automatically assuming that they’re bored, annoyed, or rejecting us,” Saline said.

That’s where clarification comes in. Uncertainty is a potent trigger for rejection sensitivity, so Saline encourages respectful questioning to address assumptions. For example, if your partner says they’re not upset but their tone sounds irritated, ask, “I’m hearing something different in your tone. Is there something you’d like to talk about?”

#9588. New Research Strengthens the Case for Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD Criteria

The new “severe-combined” ADHD subtype identified in a landmark study is marked by emotional dysregulation, a symptom the DSM-5 doesn’t include in its diagnostic criteria.

When the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was updated in 2022, officials believed that research was lacking to expand ADHD’s definition to include the common and extremely impairing symptom of emotional dysregulation. Consequently, the overwhelming and uncontrollable emotions reported by many patients remain largely unrecognized as ADHD manifestations.

Now research appears to be catching up to patient reports.

A new landmark study has revealed three ADHD subtypes that reflect neurobiological differences: predominantly inattentive; predominantly hyperactive/impulsive; and the new severe-combined, which is marked by emotional dysregulation.1

Using neuroimaging and computational modeling to map the pathways of ADHD, researchers found that the severe-combined type had 45 areas of brain abnormality tied to emotion and control compared with 26 each for the two other types. The study, which analyzed 1,154 brain scans of children and adolescents with ADHD, was published recently in JAMA Psychiatry.

The findings are “an example of recent insights emerging from neuroimaging that may impact clinical care, which has been an elusive goal,” says F. Xavier Castellanos, M.D., professor emeritus of child and adolescent psychiatry at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine. He was part of the working group that contributed to the DSM-5.

[Get This Free Download: Emotional Regulation & Anger Management Scripts]

“Still, it’s too early to assume that their intriguing results are real in the sense of replicating repeatedly in independent datasets, particularly by investigators who are not allied or collaborating with the original research team,” says Castellanos. He, like the study authors, calls for prospective studies to validate their biotypes and determine whether they may influence treatment.

Findings that reveal a new severe-combined subtype may come as no surprise to the thousands of parents of children with ADHD, and adults with the condition, who have named emotional dysregulation as the most impairing feature of ADHD in ADDitude surveys.

But, as David Anderson, Ph.D., senior psychologist at the ADHD and Behavior Disorders Center at the Child Mind Institute, points out, parents’ anecdotal feedback precedes scientific validation.

“Finding evidence of a subtype in the brain leaves open questions about the balance of nature versus nurture. Is there a biological basis for subtypes and is it reliable across the span of development?” Anderson asks. “Emotion dysregulation can be biological for kids who are more prone to emotional behavior from an early age, while some are frustrated with the world due to negative feedback they’ve gotten since kindergarten, so it’s environmental. There are multiple pathways to come to this.”

[Read: The Key to ADHD Emotional Regulation? Cultivating Gratitude, Pride & Compassion]

If the study’s findings are replicated, Castellanos says, it would become a new presentation in a future version of the DSM. “I served on the DSM-5 committee, and we were explicitly reminded that the DSM follows the field; it does not lead it. It’s only when the scientific evidence is strongly supportive that DSM changes are allowed. Otherwise, it’s too disruptive.”

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., distinguished professor at SUNY Upstate Medical University, said he believes that emotional dysregulation was not included in the DSM-5 because it might have made differential diagnosis with anxiety and mood disorders more difficult, especially in primary care. He also said he was skeptical that ADHD can be divided into biological subtypes, adding that underlying ADHD brain mechanisms exist along a spectrum and do not fall neatly into separate categories.

The study’s researchers said the findings may eventually create a path toward developing personalized therapeutic strategies.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

#9587. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

#9586. Houston cancer centre expands its art collection and curatorial ambitions

A view of the waiting room in MD Anderson's Colorectal Cancer Center, with David Aylsworth's painting Fraughter Than I Thought (2023) and the installation Carried by the Breeze by Shane Allbritton Courtesy MD Anderson

As more and more research indicates art can play an important role in health, healing and improving outcomes in medical spaces, the world’s largest cancer treatment centre is embarking on an ambitious expansion of its art collection, with plans to integrate contemporary works into new and renovated facilities as part of a broader effort to rethink the patient experience.

The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, considered one of the top cancer centres in the US, has long maintained a collection made up of classic, inoffensive “hospital art”, such as pleasant pastoral scenes. But in January 2025, it launched a contemporary art initiative focused on acquiring ambitious fine art. Since then, with the help of Jennifer Finkel, MD Anderson’s associate vice president for art experience, the institution has added nearly 300 works to a collection that already included approximately 9,000 objects.

The art initiative is part of a $2.9bn expansion across MD Anderson’s facilities in the Texas Medical Center in Houston, the largest medical complex in the world, alongside other regional and research developments scheduled for completion between 2027 and 2032. The construction projects provide an opportunity to commission site-specific works and build a collection that is integrated into the architecture, rather than simply hung on hospital walls.

“With all of the growth and new buildings, this is an opportunity to create a world-class art collection,” says Finkel, who previously held positions at Cleveland Clinic and Wake Forest University. “We're the number one cancer centre, and we deliver world-class care and research. Now it's time for our environment to really match.”

A view of a hallway in the Colorectal Cancer Center Courtesy MD Anderson

The initiative combines traditional acquisitions with site-specific commissions. Funding comes from a percent-for-art model based on construction costs, alongside philanthropic support and qualifying art donations. If 1% of the $2.9bn expansion were allocated to art, as is standard, that would amount to $29m, although the total budget for the art collection initiative has not been publicly disclosed.

The goal is to build the collection alongside the new facilities, “really integrating art into the fabric of the buildings and having this art collection be part of our culture and our in our DNA”, Finkel says.

“It's an opportunity to relook at the patient experience with art being a cornerstone of that, which is exciting,” she says. “As we renovate our older facilities, that's also an opportunity to bring new art and think about art and design cohesively in those older spaces as well.”

A hospital presents particular challenges for a curator. Works displayed in waiting rooms, corridors and examination rooms may be encountered during some of the most difficult moments in a person's life, amid the uncertainty, disappointment and hope that accompany cancer treatment. The aim is to select art that can offer patients opportunities for reflection and distraction, while contributing to their emotional wellbeing, Finkel says.

Research into the effects of art and cultural engagement on health has grown in recent years, with studies examining how art in healthcare environments can support wellbeing and help reduce anxiety. For MD Anderson, the challenge is to translate those broader findings into decisions about individual works and the spaces in which they will be displayed.

“Is it uplifting? Is it hopeful? I really like art where you can get lost in something. It can be a little bit challenging, maybe, when you're decoding something. You can spend time with it—the art can reveal itself over time,” Finkel says.

That last consideration is particularly relevant for patients who return to the hospital frequently over weeks or months, and a work that initially seems familiar may offer a new perspective with repeated encounters.

“Thinking about art, when you look at something and you've probably looked at it 50 times, and it might be the 51st, you're like, ‘Oh, I didn't see that’,” Finkel says.

The selection process also takes into account the clinical context, the demographics of patients and the length of time they are likely to spend in a particular space. A corridor through which people pass quickly calls for different considerations from a waiting room where patients might sit for an hour or longer. Colour and imagery can also be sensitive issues: Finkel considers whether certain shades of red or imagery that is “too cellular” might be unsettling for someone undergoing cancer treatment.

“I really obsess about each artwork and how someone can respond,” Finkel says. “But at the end of the day, with good contemporary art, people bring what they're going to bring and see what they're going to see in it, and you can't control that. That's part of the beauty.”

The curatorial approach is informed by the people who will use each facility. When planning the collection for MD Anderson's new Colorectal Cancer Center, Finkel initially assumed that its patients would largely be older adults. She learned that one-third of patients were between the ages of 35 and 45, prompting her to reconsider the kinds of works that might resonate in the space.

Straight Lines 30 (2021) By Mara Held at the MD Anderson Cancer Center Courtesy of the artist and Seven Sisters Gallery, photo by Charles Benton

Finkel is soon to begin work on the collection for a new dedicated prostate cancer clinic. Although its patients will predominantly be men, she is also keeping in mind their caregivers and other people who may accompany them.

The process begins before patients even reach a treatment room. Finkel considers the anxiety that can build during a hospital visit, from entering the parking garage to navigating waiting areas and undergoing examinations or procedures. “How can art be a companion on that journey?” she asks.

Wayfinding is another practical consideration. A particularly colourful print, for example, can help visitors recognise an elevator or exit in the sprawling medical complex, making a work of art a useful visual marker as well.

Finkel says MD Anderson acquires much of the collection through commercial galleries and art fairs, with an emphasis on practising artists and diverse representation. She is also quick to support artists and dealers based in Houston, where MD Anderson's local expansion offers opportunities to connect the institution's collection with the city's contemporary art scene.

At this year's edition of Untitled Art Houston earlier this month, MD Anderson dedicated $20,000 to a new acquisitions prize. The selection committee chose works by Michelle Blade, represented by Night Gallery in Los Angeles, and Kelly Tapia-Chuning, represented by the Santa Fe gallery Kouri + Corrao. Other artists in the collection include Ping Zheng, represented by Houston's Seven Sisters; the Houston-based David Aylsworth, represented by Inman Gallery; and Mara Held, the daughter of the artist Al Held, who is also represented by Seven Sisters.

The initiative has also developed site-specific commissions that respond directly to their surroundings. One of the most recognisable works in the Colorectal Cancer Center is Carried by the Breeze, an installation by the local artist Shane Allbritton. Suspended above a waiting room, the sculpture comprises translucent leaves incorporating DNA-inspired patterns. The leaves move gently in the current from the air-conditioning system, reflecting light from a nearby window across the ceiling and walls.

The work was made using a specially selected plastic that is easier to clean and resistant to dust, illustrating how the demands of a clinical environment must shape the materials and construction of a commission. The project also carried personal significance for Allbritton's family: her mother, who was part of the family team that helped realise the artist's designs, was diagnosed with ovarian cancer.

“Anytime we can contribute to the comfort level of patients who are entering a space that may be filled with anxiety and uncertainty, it’s important to have environmental features that are comforting, that are handmade, that are creatively expressing something that gives them inspiration or hope,” Allbritton said in a video produced for the hospital.

“Artists want to be a part of this collection because there is that impact on someone's health,” Finkel says. “When they're going through probably one of the scariest times of their lives, and to be part of that, it's really impactful.”

Beyond the acquisition and display of works, MD Anderson encourages patients and visitors to engage with the collection. Works on display in facilities have wall labels, and the collection has its own focused interactive guide on the Bloomberg Connects app, allowing people to learn more about the art while they wait for treatment. Finkel says the hospital's partners at Bloomberg have relayed that they have been “astounded” by the level of engagement.

The plans extend beyond the visual arts. MD Anderson is developing a performing arts programme drawing on Houston's symphony, ballet and other cultural organisations. Finkel is also interested in establishing an artist-in-residence programme that could encompass visual artists, poets or musicians.

“It's not just about hanging the art,” Finkel says. “We’re thinking about those other levels that people can engage with the art while they're here.”

More than 200 works on view at Henrique Faria Fine Art are on offer to raise funds for emergency aid in Venezuela through the World Central Kitchen

The latest “Survey of Global Collecting” from Art Basel and UBS also found a growing number of buyers are bypassing dealers and auction houses to purchase directly from artists

The new grant, funded by the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation and the Rema Hort Mann Fund, supports New York City artists undergoing cancer treatment

Combined, the prizes will provide as much as $113,200 for acquisitions at the fair

#9585. How to define cheating in a relationship (and what to do about it)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Late-night texts lighting up their phone. A “friend from work” who comes up a little too often when they talk about their day. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and it’s a name you've conveniently left out of your story. Either way, it leads to a quiet, nagging sense that something's off.

Some cheating is obvious. But the old idea that it only counts if it's physical doesn't hold up to how people experience betrayal today. Emotional connections can form through a screen, and it isn't always a single, clear-cut act.

Here’s the big picture on what cheating really means, and what to do if you’re facing it in your own relationship.

Cheating means acting in a way that violates the boundaries and trust that a couple has built together.

The issue is that the boundaries aren’t always clear. Many couples never discuss what's off limits, whether that’s a text to an ex, a close emotional friendship, or a flirtatious dinner. You and your partner may share the same values, and assume you’re aligned on the specifics. Then a moment reveals you’re not.

Where people draw the line on cheating usually traces back to a few underlying factors.

Attachment style: People prone to relationship anxiety may read more behaviors as threatening. People who lean more avoidant may downplay concerning behavior as trivial, including their own.

Cultural and religious background: Some cultures and religions view certain dating norms, like close friendships outside the relationship, as completely normal, while others see them as concerning.

Relationship structure: Couples set their own rules for the relationship, whether that’s monogamy, non-monogamy, or somewhere in between. Those rules define what counts as betrayal.

Related read: How to find your attachment style and deepen your relationships

Infidelity takes many forms, and even within each form, it can look drastically different depending on the situation. Here’s how it tends to show up.

This is the one most people picture first: romantic or sexual contact with someone outside the relationship, without your partner knowing or agreeing to it. That last part is key.

Couples in open relationships can have very different lines. As long as both partners are on the same page, physical intimacy with others can be a normal part of the relationship.

Emotional cheating means forming a close bond with someone outside your relationship that pulls closeness or energy away from your partner.

The line between a close friendship and an emotional affair can feel blurry, but research points to three signs:

Details get shared that don't get shared with your partner.

An unspoken attraction exists, even if neither person names it.

Emotional cheating can be dismissed because nothing physical happened, but many people find it just as painful as physical infidelity, sometimes more so. It tends to build slowly, until the loyalty has quietly shifted.

Virtual cheating is physical or emotional cheating through a screen. This can look like sexting, intimate messaging, or building a close connection online. Some therapists also include excessive pornography use when it's hidden and gets in the way of intimacy with a partner, though opinions vary.

This type of cheating is more accessible than most other forms of infidelity, and is often harder to catch. A message is one tap away, at any hour, with virtually anyone.

Micro-cheating involves smaller, ambiguous behaviors that fall short of the categories above, but can still chip away at trust. Some common examples include:

Keeping a dating profile active "just in case"

Finding constant reasons to message one specific person

Spending time with someone without mentioning it to your partner

Flirting with someone in a way you wouldn't if your partner were present

It comes down to whether it's a repeated pattern your partner wouldn't be okay with.

Financial infidelity means hiding money, concealing debt, keeping secret accounts, or making big financial decisions without telling your partner. It's a serious trust issue, especially in long-term relationships where finances are shared.

This is more common than most people expect and can do just as much damage as other forms of infidelity.

If you’re suspicious of your partner, sitting with that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But before you act on a hunch, try slowing down and approaching the situation with as much calm as you can.

Start by noticing what’s actually happening—and what’s actually changed—versus what you suspect. Has your partner’s communication, availability, or emotional presence shifted in a specific way? Or is this more of a gut sense that something's off?

Both are valid, but knowing which one you’re dealing with can help you decide how to proceed.

💙 Explore Sensations vs. Emotions with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your unease may not be about your suspicions. It might be disconnection, feeling unappreciated, or a sense that something’s changed between you. Getting clear on what’s bugging you before you bring it up can make the conversation more productive.

💙 Dig deeper with Investigating Anxiety from the Emotions Series on Calm.

You may think that checking their phone, socials, or location data will settle your suspicion about the situation. But it tends to worsen your anxiety.

If you find something, you’re left dealing with what you found and the fact that you went looking. If you don’t, the relief rarely lasts, because whatever made you suspicious in the first place is still unresolved.

A few minutes of focused breathing before a hard conversation can settle your body and quiet your mind. That short reset can help you feel steadier and lead to a clearer conversation for both of you.

💙 Take a Pause to Breathe on the Calm app.

Before you bring something up, think about what you’re hoping for. Do you want clarity? Reassurance? That goal can keep you focused, even if the conversation gets derailed.

Approaching the discussion with an open mind, rather than jumping to accusations, often invites a more honest exchange.

Instead of starting with “I think you’re cheating on me,” try something along the lines of “I’ve been feeling disconnected and I’d like to talk about it.”

Whether you're dealing with confirmed infidelity or unresolved suspicion, you don't have to process it alone. Support from a therapist, individually or as a couple, can offer a structured space to work through it.

Sometimes suspicion itself, even without proof of cheating, may be a sign that the relationship needs attention.

Cheating is a violation of the spoken or unspoken agreements you and your partner have made about exclusivity. It can show up physically, emotionally, or virtually, and what counts can look different from couple to couple. Secrecy and broken trust are usually the common thread.

Read more: Here's how to work through the most common relationship issues

The main types of cheating are physical, emotional, and virtual, though subtler patterns such as financial secrecy or "micro-cheating" can apply too.

Physical cheating involves intimate contact outside the relationship. Emotional cheating involves a close bond kept hidden from your partner. Virtual cheating involves a romantic connection through a screen.

Emotional cheating can feel just as harmful as physical cheating, and for some people, more so. It often builds slowly, through shared thoughts and private moments your partner doesn't know about.

Physical cheating usually involves specific, identifiable moments, while emotional cheating often unfolds gradually, as loyalty fades over time.

Cheating almost always involves some kind of concealment. Being vague, withholding details, or keeping a connection secret are all forms of it. Sometimes it's the hiding, more than the act itself, that turns it into a betrayal.

Couples can define cheating differently, based on their values, culture, and the specific agreements they've made. Partners in open relationships, for example, may knowingly allow behaviors that other couples wouldn't. What’s important is that you and your partner are on the same page about boundaries.

Disagreements over what’s considered cheating are worth addressing head-on. A transparent conversation about your expectations and boundaries can feel uncomfortable, but it's one of the more protective things you can do for a relationship. A couples therapist can support this conversation if it feels overwhelming to navigate alone.

When you’re talking to your partner about what’s bothering you, try focusing on your own experience rather than their behavior. Something like "I've been feeling distant and want to check in with us" opens the door for an honest conversation instead of a defensive one.

In some cases, trust can be rebuilt after cheating, though it takes consistent effort from both of you. Many couples find professional support helpful along the way.

It usually requires transparency and accountability to understand what led to the breach. Leaving is a valid choice too, as long as the decision is made carefully.

Read more: Recovering from infidelity: 6 tips to help couples heal from an affair

#9584. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9583. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9582. 2,500-year-old solar observatory identified in Mexico

The recently identified 2,500-year-old solar observatory at Teteles de Ávila Castillo in Puebla, Mexico Photo: Alberto Diez Barroso Repizo, INAH

An 11-year-long archaeological project at Teteles de Ávila Castillo, in Puebla’s Sierra Norte in east-central Mexico, may shed new light on ancient cultural interactions in Mesoamerica. Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) recently announced that the research team there has identified a 2,500-year-old solar observatory. It could be the region's first of its kind. Other findings include ceramic offerings, infant remains inside a ceramic vessel and numerous obsidian objects.

Teteles reflects the challenges of protecting archaeological heritage on privately owned land. Discovered in 1939, the nine-hectare site remained in private hands for decades, during which time it was looted and damaged. In 2007, its owner donated 3.5 hectares to INAH. Research began in 2015 with support from the civil association Tzoncóyotl, but the remaining land is still private property, limiting excavation there.

The site’s 16 pre-Hispanic pyramidal structures show several phases of occupation. “Teteles flourished during the Middle Preclassic period (900BC-600BC) but declined around AD100, possibly because nearby Cantona expanded,” Alberto Diez Barroso Repizo, Teteles’s archaeological project director, tells The Art Newspaper.

“Green obsidian beads found in offerings containing infant remains suggest connections with Teotihuacan,” Diez adds, “which controlled the Hidalgo quarry where the obsidian originated.” He says other human remains may have decayed because of harsh weather conditions, and the variety of obsidian objects could indicate that Teteles’s inhabitants produced and sold obsidian utensils. “Teteles lay along an active trade route, facilitating cultural exchange,” Diez says.

Even after the area was largely abandoned, ritual offerings continued to be placed at the site, suggesting that it may have become a pilgrimage destination. Diez links the offerings to the Totonac culture, which flourished in Mexico’s Sierra Norte region and along the northern Gulf Coast. “Totonac ceramic offerings and a sculpture fragment dating from AD600 to AD900 suggest that later groups may have regarded Teteles's former inhabitants as their ancestors,” he says, pointing to the possible origins of Totonac culture.

Some of the artefacts found at the site Courtesy the Archaeological Project of Teteles de Ávila Castillo, INAH

The structure identified as a solar observatory could point to early Maya-Huastec connections previously suggested by linguistic studies. “The observatory resembles E-Group complexes (structures associated with solar observations) at Maya sites like Uaxactún in Guatemala,” Diez says. “It is the first of its kind identified in northern Puebla, though La Venta's Olmec complex may be older.” He adds that its alignments could relate to the Mesoamerican agricultural calendar.

Diez also emphasises the astronomical significance of the site's main 12m-tall pyramid: “It may be aligned with Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky, associated with the beginning of the Mesoamerican calendar in February.” He notes that although scholars have studied this alignment in Mesopotamian and Egyptian structures, its significance in Mesoamerica remains underexplored.

The archaeologist Ivan Šprajc—an archaeoastronomy expert at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana (who was not involved in the project)—places Teteles within a broader tradition of earlier ceremonial complexes he has studied. “Previous archaeoastronomical studies using Lidar technology have documented similar and earlier complexes along the southern Gulf and Pacific coasts,” he says, “some dating to the late Early Preclassic period”, before 1000BC.

Šprajc is cautious about using the term “observatory”. “The common practice of referring to these complexes as observatories is not entirely justifiable,” he says. “Although they contain astronomical alignments, their primary functions were ceremonial or residential, and such alignments were commonly incorporated in very different types of structures throughout Mesoamerica.” He adds that solar alignments tied to the ceremonial agricultural cycle were common, though the calendar year's start shifted over time.

Further research, including comparative studies and artefact analysis, will certainly reveal more about these discoveries in the future. “Plans are underway to open the site and a museum to the public,” Diez says, although an exact timeline is pending.

#9581. How to dream more: 6 tips to increase how often you dream

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We all know that one person who says, “You’ll never believe what I dreamt last night!” Many people who dream can become obsessed with the stories their minds show them at night. Some people believe their dreams provide insights into their subconscious, while others say they inspire creativity. And those who aren’t into the deep dream interpretation simply like the fantasy world that their minds create when they’re asleep.

If you’re fascinated by your dreams for any of these reasons, you might want to learn how to dream more and make your dreams more vivid. And while you can’t control everything—like the inevitable falling nightmare everyone has had at least once—you can do things to dream more frequently and to make those dreams easier to recall. Here are a few simple techniques and lifestyle changes you might want to try to make the most of the time you spend asleep.

When you sleep better, you’re more likely to enter the rapid eye movement (REM) part of your sleep cycle, when most dreaming occurs. This sleep cycle may increase the chances of having more frequent and vivid dreams, so here are a few tips to encourage deeper sleep.

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help regulate your sleep cycle and increase the likelihood of dreaming. To get enough REM sleep, aim for 7–9 hours of sleep each night.

💙 Try relaxing an hour before bed with Soften Into Sleep, a meditation that can help you release tension at night.

Read, take a warm bath, or practice mindfulness to ease into rest and create an environment for dreaming. Avoid screens for at least an hour before bed, as the blue light can disrupt your body’s natural sleep-wake cycle. If you must use devices, try a blue light filter or dim your screen.

💙 Explore these nine tips to help you build a better bedtime routine.

To improve sleep quality and increase your chances of dreaming, keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. The ideal temperature is about 60–67 degrees Fahrenheit (or 15–19 degrees Celsius). Use blackout curtains to block light, earplugs or a white noise machine to drown out noise, and invest in a comfortable mattress and pillows to support your posture.

Lastly, keep your bedroom tidy and use it only for sleep and relaxation if you can. This can help you create a mental association between your bedroom and restful sleep.

💙 Press play on one of our relaxing Soundscapes, like White Noise Ocean Surf, to help you drift off to sleep.

Practice meditation, yoga, or deep breathing exercises to help decrease anxiety so you can get a good night’s sleep, which may promote more vivid dreaming. Regular exercise can help too, but remember to avoid vigorous activity too close to bedtime.

💙 Keep stress at bay by tuning into 7 Days of Managing Stress, a stress reduction series hosted by Tamara Levitt.

Heavy meals, caffeine, or alcohol before bed can disrupt sleep and decrease dream frequency. Opt for light snacks if you're hungry, and avoid caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime.

💙 Add mindfulness to mealtime with our session on the Benefits of Mindful Eating.

Drink water throughout the day to support sleep quality, but try to limit water intake about an hour before bed to prevent trips to the bathroom in the middle of the night.

During your wind down routine, you can sip teas like chamomile or valerian root. These are thought to have calming effects that may promote relaxation and improve sleep quality, which may lead to more vivid dreams.

💙 Listen to a relaxing Sleep Story before bed, like Why Do We Sleep, while sipping tea as part of a new nighttime ritual.

Sleep is divided into several stages that cycle throughout the night, typically lasting about 90 minutes per cycle.

Stage 1 (light sleep): This is a transitional phase where you drift in and out of sleep.

Stage 2 (deeper light sleep): Your body temperature drops and your heart rate begins to slow.

Stage 3 (deep sleep): Known as slow-wave sleep, this stage promotes physical recovery and health.

REM sleep: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, where your brain activity increases and your eyes move rapidly under your eyelids, is when the most vivid dreams occur.

Melatonin is a hormone your body naturally produces that helps to regulate your sleep-wake cycles. Levels rise in the evening to help you feel sleepy and decrease in the morning to help you wake up. Some people take melatonin supplements to help with sleep issues like insomnia, jet lag, or other sleep disorders, but it may also affect your dreams.

Some studies suggest that melatonin may enhance REM sleep. This might lead to more frequent and vivid dreams, and some people who take melatonin report more intense and memorable dreams.

Melatonin may also help with dream recall by enhancing overall sleep quality.

The effect of melatonin on dreams can vary from person to person. Remember to always consult a medical professional before you take any supplement, as they can interact with other medications or simply not be right for you.

People like remembering their dreams for a number of reasons. Perhaps it sparks their curiosity about what they could be feeling on a subconscious level or could provide them with an escape from reality. Whatever your reason for wanting to remember your dreams may be, dream recall can become easier and more natural with time and practice.

Keep a dream journal: Write down your dreams as soon as you wake up, even if you can only remember bits and pieces of them. Over time, this can train your brain to pay more attention to your dreams. Review your dream journal during the day to help reinforce your memory and increase your chances of remembering future dreams.

Set an intention: Before you go to sleep, reinforce your desire to remember your dreams. Repeating a phrase like "I will remember my dreams" may increase your chances of recalling them when you wake up.

Stay still upon waking: Moving too quickly when you wake up can cause you to forget your dreams, so before you get out of bed, lie still for a few moments and try to focus on your dream. Sometimes a single image or emotion can trigger the memory of the entire dream.

Reflect on your day: Before bed, think about your day and journal about it. This can help create a connection between your waking and dreaming life and associate both with memories and self-reflection. Thus, this practice may make it easier to remember your dreams.

Practice mindfulness: Regular mindfulness and meditation practice can improve your overall awareness and attention, including your ability to remember dreams. Meditate before bed to clear your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. These six tips for meditating in bed can help you get started.

Wake up naturally: Waking up suddenly can startle you into thinking intensely about the here and now, making it harder to remember dreams, so try to avoid using an alarm clock if you can. Pay attention to your body's natural sleep cycles and try to go to bed early enough to wake up naturally. If you need an alarm, set one that wakes you gently, perhaps with soft sounds or a sunrise effect.

Vivid dreams can be more engaging and memorable than other forms of dreaming that are less detailed.

Before falling asleep, visualize a recent dream or imagine a scenario you’d like to dream about in as much detail as possible. This can help stimulate your mind and lead to more vivid dreams.

Experiment with different sleeping positions to see if they influence the vividness of your dreams.

Get natural light during the day and reduce light exposure before bed to help regulate your sleep cycle and improve the quality of your REM sleep. Improving your sleep cycles and natural circadian rhythm may lead to more vivid dreams.

Creative activities like drawing, writing, or playing music can stimulate your imagination and enhance your dreams.

Meditate before bed to help calm your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. This may increase the chances of having vivid dreams. As you’re releasing stresses from the day, you may create space for your subconscious mind to flourish as you rest. These 10 mindful activities can help you release stress quickly at the end of the day.

Some people use supplements like galantamine, choline, or vitamin B6 to try to enhance dream vividness. Consult a healthcare provider before using any supplements, as they can have side effects and interactions with other medications you’re already taking.

Once you’re remembering your dreams most mornings, you might get curious about steering them. That’s lucid dreaming: knowing you’re dreaming while it’s happening, which can let you look around, change the scene, or just enjoy the ride.

It takes practice, and it doesn’t happen for everyone. The good news is that things you may already be doing, like keeping a dream journal and setting an intention before bed, are also how many people start learning it.

If you’re curious, our step-by-step guide can help you learn how to lucid dream, with techniques like reality checks, MILD, and wake back to bed.

Certain foods and nutrients may influence your dreaming patterns. For example, foods containing tryptophan, like turkey and dairy products, can promote sleepiness and may impact the quality of your dreams. Foods rich in vitamin B6, like bananas, chickpeas, fish, and fortified cereals, may help with recall.

Eat a balanced diet with a variety of nutrients to support your overall sleep health, and avoid heavy meals and caffeine close to bedtime, as they can disrupt sleep and reduce dream frequency.

Several factors can affect your ability to remember dreams.

Poor sleep quality, such as disruptions in your sleep cycle, can hinder dream recall.

Stress or anxiety can interfere with sleep and make it harder to remember your dreams.

Sleep disorders like insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome disrupt sleep and impact dream recall.

Some medications, particularly those that affect the central nervous system, can interfere with dreaming.

Alcohol and drugs can alter sleep patterns and reduce the likelihood of remembering dreams.

A lack of interest in dreams can mean the brain doesn’t focus on retaining them.

Sleep disorders can significantly impact dreaming. Insomnia, which makes it difficult to fall or stay asleep, can reduce the amount of REM sleep you get, leading to fewer dreams and poorer dream recall.

Sleep apnea causes repeated interruptions in breathing during sleep, disrupting REM sleep cycles and reducing the frequency and vividness of dreams. Treatments like CPAP therapy for sleep apnea may improve sleep quality and dreaming.

Restless leg syndrome can also interfere with falling and staying asleep, which can impact dream frequency and recall.

Narcolepsy is marked by excessive daytime sleepiness and fragmented nighttime sleep. It may lead to vivid (and sometimes bizarre) dreams or dream-like hallucinations.

Generally, there are few risks to trying to dream more. Supplements like melatonin or galantamine may cause side effects or interact with other medications, so talk to your doctor before taking them.

Paying more attention to your dreams can sometimes lead to more vivid nightmares, especially if you have underlying anxiety or stress.

Understanding your dreams may reveal hidden thoughts, fears, and desires, and can help process emotions, particularly those you may not fully address during waking life. This may help in emotional healing.

Dreams can also offer creative solutions to problems or provide new perspectives for challenges you face in waking life.

#9580. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

#9578. Wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

Researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin have created a soft wearable patch that improved REM sleep in real-world testing without medication or surgery. Known as NEUSLeeP, the device combines gentle ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that track brain activity as it happens. This allows the patch to influence deep areas of the brain involved in sleep while also monitoring the brain's response.

"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort. "Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering, who supervised Tang's work and served as the principal investigator (PI) directing the overall project.

Wearable Patch Helps People Reach REM Faster

The researchers tested the technology in a study involving 28 people, with the results published in Nature Communications. On average, participants entered REM sleep 43 minutes sooner and remained in that stage for about 16 minutes longer.

The benefits were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing some sleep difficulties. Users also described the patch as comfortable and safe, and the study reported minimal adverse effects.

Possible Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health

Among healthy participants, NEUSLeeP stimulation also increased heart rate variability, which is commonly used as an indicator of the body's ability to respond to stress. Brain imaging revealed changes in circuits associated with emotion, raising the possibility that the technology could support mood regulation and psychological resilience.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."

REM sleep disruptions have been associated with depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Current approaches to sleep problems, including medication and behavioral therapy, may cause side effects or may not directly address the underlying factors that interfere with REM sleep.

Future Trials for Insomnia, Depression and PTSD

The team plans to conduct larger studies to verify the initial results and evaluate whether NEUSLeeP could help people with PTSD, depression and chronic insomnia. The researchers also see potential uses in home sleep monitoring, neuroscience research and personalized sleep treatments.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."

Researchers Move Toward Commercialization

The team is collaborating with Discovery to Impact, UT's commercialization unit, in an effort to move the technology toward the market. A patent application has also been filed for the device.

Other team members are William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

#9577. In a friends-with-benefits relationship (FWB)? 6 tips to know

A friendship has turned physical, but everything else seems to be staying the same. You grab dinner, send memes, and share inside jokes, all with the understanding that it’s just casual. And yet, you can’t help but wonder where things are headed.

Friends-with-benefits relationships sit in the gray area between friendship and romance. These arrangements work out well for some people, but for others, they slowly become a source of anxiety or hurt.

Whether you're already in one or just curious what you'd be signing up for, here's a closer look at what a friends-with-benefits relationship involves — the risks and the rewards, plus how to navigate one with grace and self-awareness.

A friends-with-benefits relationship (often shortened to FWB) is when two friends are also physically involved with each other, without the commitment or expectations that come with a romantic partnership. There's no exclusivity agreement (unless discussed), no defined future together, and usually none of the relationship milestones that come with dating.

The idea is that the friendship stays intact while you enjoy the physical side of a relationship, no strings attached. It may sound straightforward, but in practice, it usually takes more communication and honesty than people expect going in.

Every FWB relationship looks different. Some see each other regularly, while others keep it more sporadic. What they generally have in common is a mutual understanding that neither person is looking for something more serious.

Not sure if you’re in one? Here are some signs that point toward a FWB dynamic:

You skip the things typical couples do, like meeting each other's families or planning trips together.

You haven’t talked about exclusivity or where the relationship is headed.

You call each other “friends” when describing your situation to others.

You’re dating, or open to dating, other people.

The relationship stays undefined, and one or both of you is comfortable keeping it that way.

Like any relationship structure, being friends with benefits has its upsides and its risks. If you're deciding whether to start a FWB relationship, this list is a good gut check for whether the upsides outweigh the risks for you.

Physical intimacy without the pressure of commitment

Closeness and companionship that come from an existing friendship

More freedom to focus on other priorities, like your career, personal growth, or social life

Low-stakes exploration if you’re not ready for something serious

Clarity about what you want (or don’t want) from relationships

One-sided feelings that go unnoticed or unspoken

Ambiguity about what the relationship actually is, even as time passes

Jealousy, especially if one of you starts dating someone else

Damage to the friendship if it ends badly

Lack of communication about needs due to unclear expectations

FWB relationships don't come with a rulebook — but there are common threads among the ones that work: honesty, self-awareness, and ongoing communication. These tips follow those threads.

FWB tension often comes from mismatched expectations that were never discussed. Before you get physically involved—or as soon as possible if you already are—have an open conversation about what you both want.

Get clear about what “casual” means to each of you, and make sure you're both comfortable with it. Talking through this early beats untangling confusion later.

💙 For more guidance, here’s how to set healthy boundaries in relationships.

Unless you've agreed otherwise, friends-with-benefits arrangements are usually non-exclusive, meaning either of you could be dating or getting involved with someone else. It's worth discussing up front how you'll handle that — will you tell each other when someone new is in the picture?

Your feelings about a FWB setup might shift over time. Take a moment every so often to check in on how you're feeling about the situation.

A few minutes of reflection, or a short meditation, can help you notice any uncomfortable feelings you've been avoiding.

💙 Try Checking In With Yourself with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

Without active effort, the friendship side of FWB can slowly fade into the background until only the physical side is left.

Make it a point to spend time together without getting intimate. Ask about different parts of their life. Show up for each other the way you would have before your dynamic changed.

💙 Learn more about Mindful Friendships with Jay Shetty on Calm.

A FWB arrangement that works one month might not work the next. People's feelings and circumstances naturally evolve with time. The key is speaking up when you notice a change, whether it’s on your end or theirs.

This is where these relationships often get complicated. One of you has a change of heart, but stays silent, afraid of disrupting the dynamic or losing the other person.

Being upfront can be uncomfortable, but it’s one of the most respectful things you can do for yourself and your friend.

💙 Press play on Say What You Need to Say with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Any friends-with-benefits relationship could end at some point, and thinking ahead about how you'd handle it can reduce the fallout. Think about whether preserving the friendship matters to you. Either way, expect some awkwardness afterward.

It can be hard to end things with care and honesty, but it does less damage to the friendship than silence or avoidance.

Knowing what to do in a FWB situation matters, but it’s equally important to be aware of what can trip you up.

Don't assume you're on the same page without checking. Shared silence isn't shared understanding.

Don't use the arrangement as a way to stay close to someone you have feelings for. That's a recipe for getting hurt.

Don't ignore your feelings because they feel inconvenient. Feelings that get dismissed tend to resurface louder later.

Don't skip the conversation about seeing other people. Assumptions here can turn this arrangement messy fast.

Don't stay in it if you’re consistently left feeling worse. A casual relationship isn't worth more than your peace of mind.

Don't expect the friendship to survive constant unspoken tension. Even close friendships have limits, and unspoken hurt can gradually erode them.

Friends with benefits means you and your friend are physically intimate without the commitments of a romantic relationship. There's no assumed exclusivity and no defined future — just a dynamic that exists somewhere between friendship and romance.

Friends-with-benefits relationships get complicated when feelings become one-sided. One of you may develop deeper feelings while the other doesn't. It can also get tricky when expectations shift without a conversation, when one of you starts dating someone else, or when the physical side starts overshadowing the friendship.

There's no set timeline for a FWB relationship. Some arrangements last a few months, while others go on for years. How long yours lasts depends on whether you’re both comfortable with it, communication stays open, and your feelings stay compatible over time.

Friends with benefits may be a good idea if you and the other person are aligned on what you’re looking for. It can be a comfortable, low-pressure arrangement, or a source of confusion and hurt if expectations aren't discussed. Open communication and regular self-reflection tend to give the relationship the best shot at working.

Yes, some FWB arrangements do evolve into committed relationships, particularly when both people develop feelings around the same time and are open to more. That said, staying in the arrangement in hopes that it'll turn into something more comes with a risk. You may end up hurt if the other person doesn't feel the same way.

Jealousy is a normal reaction, even in FWB arrangements that are meant to be casual. This happens because intimacy can naturally lead to attachment. If you’re feeling this way, it might be a sign the situation no longer fits what you want.

The best way to end a friends-with-benefits relationship without ruining the friendship is to be direct and honest. Ghosting or avoiding the other person usually does more damage than an open conversation. Be clear about why things have changed, share appreciation for what you had, and give each other some space afterward.

#9576. Pop-up tattoo studio opens at Amsterdam's Rembrandt House Museum

Left: Tattoo artists Rupa van Teylingen, Henk Schiffmacher, Tycho Veldhoen, and Timothy John Englisch at the Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam. Right: Rembrandt’s The Descent from the Cross (1633) Photo: Mark Bolk, courtesy of Schiffmacher and Veldhoen/Museum Rembrandthuis

A young man in Amsterdam will become the lifelong owner of a free Rembrandt etching, thanks to a partnership between the Rembrandt House Museum and two Dutch tattoo studios.

In a collaboration entitled “The Poor Man’s Rembrandt Project”, tattoo artists are recreating one of Rembrandt’s most intricate etchings, The Descent from the Cross (1633), across a man’s entire back. The artwork will take 20 hours to create by a team of tattoo artists from the studios Schiffmacher & Veldhoen in Amsterdam and St. Catherina in Antwerp.

Members of the public can also book a session or drop in to the museum between 26 October-7 November to get a (smaller) Rembrandt tattoo, costing from €100 to €300, from the museum's temporary studio.

This is the second edition of the project; tattoo artists from Schiffmacher & Veldhoen first offered tattoos inspired by the Dutch master’s works in a pop-up studio at the museum in 2023.

The project is not a gimmick, according to the Rembrandt House Museum's director Milou Halbesma. “This is all about content,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “We are a museum of craftsmanship, and we are trying to throw open the craft of Rembrandt and his students as widely as possible. If you translate that to today, we have a number of world-famous Amsterdam creators… And this is a chance to get a tattoo from one of these masters.”

Some of the Rembrandt-inspired tattoo designs that visitors can request at the pop-up studio Courtesy of Museum Rembrandthuis

The tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher says that the etching—one of a series by Rembrandt focusing on the people taking Christ’s body from the cross—was particularly suitable. “We looked at other Rembrandts but this was so dramatic,” he says. “The spine almost becomes part of the cross.”

He adds that a tattoo-based interpretation of the 17th-century Dutch master is also fitting. “Rembrandt was interested in sea farers, he was a collector, and there were so many different people in Amsterdam at the time, there would have been tattooed sailors,” he says.

Bo Kwakernaak, 28, and from Amersvoort, responded to a call on Instagram to provide his body as the canvas for the The Descent from the Cross tattoo. He currently has a partial reproduction of the etching on his back, created in around ten hours, and it will be completed during a late night opening at the museum on 7 November.

“I have always felt a connection with Rembrandt paintings,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “I’m not religious, but I’ve always been drawn to religious imagery. Here, it is the emotion in the faces, the feeling of grief. There is a whole story in one image.”

When the tattoo is completed, according to Schiffmacher, the pigment needs to ‘soften’ into the skin for a year before it will look its best. “This is an etching too but the skin is different from paper,” he says. “It is the only bit of art you can take to your grave.”
