#9546. V&A proposing significant cuts to its academy amid financial pressures

The V&A has offered adult courses for decades, drawing on its collections and curators in a tradition that goes back to the museum’s origins as a school of design

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) has drawn up plans to dismantle much of the V&A Academy, a significant part of its adult-learning programme, by the end of the year, The Art Newspaper has learned. Around 50% of the Academy’s staff may be cut and the future of flagship courses are under threat. Senior figures in other parts of the museum have also been asked to propose cuts to their teams, according to people familiar with the plans.

The V&A has offered adult courses for decades, drawing on its collections and curators in a tradition that goes back to the museum’s origins as a school of design. In 2016 it launched the Learning Academy to run much of its learning programmes. It was later renamed V&A Academy, which today runs expert-led courses, practical workshops and talks. Its courses are taught mainly at the V&A’s South Kensington site and online.

The proposals for cuts to the Academy, which sits within the museum’s commercial department, were communicated to staff on 5 October and justified by management on the grounds that the programme had failed to meet income expectations, according to people with direct knowledge of the discussions. The changes would see many of the Academy’s in-person courses at South Kensington brought to an end, including flagship courses relaunched this year in a ten-week format, with a hybrid option allowing students to attend in person or online.

The Academy’s African heritage programme and professional-development courses for museum-sector workers are among the activities expected to be retained. Selected on-demand and live online courses are also expected to continue.

The consultation period for staff to discuss the proposals with management and provide feedback is due to end today (26 October), according to people with knowledge of the matter that The Art Newspaper spoke to.

The Art Newspaper has spoken to current staff members and others with knowledge of the plans, all of whom asked not to be named for fear of repercussions. “Nobody had any inkling this was going to happen,” says one staff member. Another adds that the museum is “full of people who are feeling very demoralised”. If the proposals go ahead, the Academy will cease to operate in its current form by the end of the year, according to people with knowledge of the plans.

A V&A spokesperson said in a statement sent to The Art Newspaper: “We are currently reviewing the V&A Academy offer and the way in which this is delivered as part of wider efforts to streamline activity and identify efficiencies across our operations to ensure they are financially sustainable and deliver maximum impact. We are still in the consultation phase, and no final decisions have been made, but the current proposals will see us continue to deliver an adult learning programme." The spokesperson made clear that the V&A would not be able to comment further at this time.

The proposed restructuring is striking in light of the Academy’s recent reported performance. The V&A’s 2024–25 annual report says the Academy recorded sales of £1.2m, an increase of more than 22% on the previous year, while its contribution to the museum rose by more than 60% to £365,000.

The 2025–26 annual report does not provide a full breakdown of the Academy’s annual income, expenditure or profit. Instead, it describes the Academy’s hybrid learning strategy as “combining scalable online formats with high-impact in-person art history experiences”, saying the approach expanded the programme’s “reach and resilience” during its first full year and “consolidated” the growth achieved the previous year.

The report also records that the hybrid course Arts of Japan “contributed to V&A Academy’s biggest ever quarter in spring 2026, when total sales exceeded £400,000”.

At the time of writing, one of the Academy’s five flagship 10-week hybrid courses, A History of London: 1066–1666, was marked as sold out on the museum’s website. People familiar with the proposals say all five courses, including Arts of Japan and A History of London, are expected to be discontinued.

The proposed cuts come after a series of challenges for the V&A in recent months, including allegations of racism reported byThe Art Newspaper in July and strikes over pay and working conditions in September. The disputes over conditions continue: on 19 October, the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union and Prospect announced further strike action across all four V&A sites (South Kensington, East Museum, East Storehouse and Young V&A) on 29 and 30 October. However, statements sent to The Art Newspaper today from both unions said that their members have suspended strike action, to allow for further talks after an “improved offer” from the museum.

The V&A has also launched a voluntary exit scheme open to staff across the institution, which is expected to close on 26 October, according to people with knowledge of its terms. In response to The Art Newspaper’s October report on the voluntary exit scheme, a spokesperson said inflation, economic uncertainty and reduced visitor spending were contributing to financial pressures, while below-inflation government settlements would reduce funding in real terms over the coming years. The V&A’s 2025–26 annual report records a 30% rise in retail net sales to £15.7m.

The accounts show that the museum received £59.9m in government grant-in-aid during the year, up from £56.2m in 2024–25 and representing 42% of the group’s income. A further £5.2m was awarded through the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund to support essential work to protect the buildings at South Kensington and Young V&A.

The proposals to make cuts at the Academy come against the backdrop of a major expansion of the V&A’s estate, including the opening of V&A East Storehouse in May 2025 and V&A East Museum in April 2026. Some staff believe the South Kensington museum is bearing the cost of expenditure associated with the new east London sites. “We suspect that the South Kensington site is paying for the financial problems associated with V&A East,” says one staff member.

Prospect’s national secretary for heritage, Paula Lamont, tells The Art Newspaper in a statement: “Our members are concerned that the financial cost of opening new sites is falling on them, rather than being absorbed in other areas. Heaping more workload and pressure on an increasingly demoralised workforce is unsustainable and cannot be the answer.”

According to a report by Arts Professional, the PCS union has claimed that the institution is projecting cumulative operational deficits of £19m by 2030. The V&A did not address the figure when asked by The Art Newspaper. Its latest annual report rates the risk to longer-term financial sustainability as high. It says: “Mitigations through commercial growth and cost reduction have been identified and form a central tenet of the V&A’s new five-year strategy 2026-30.”

The terms offered to V&A Academy staff remain unclear, with concerns that those with less than two years’ service may not qualify for statutory redundancy pay under UK law. The Academy has around 17 permanent staff, but its courses also feature guest lecturers from across the museum and beyond. According to information available via the V&A’s website, for 12 of the Academy’s courses this autumn, five hybrid and seven online-only, there are around 100 lecturers and speakers besides Academy staff, from curators elsewhere in the V&A to freelance lecturers and visiting academics, suggesting the effects of any cuts could be felt far outside the Academy.

Staff are also concerned about proposed cuts to teams across the wider museum, believed to be around 10-15%, which are expected to affect curatorial roles. A former senior member of staff who witnessed the V&A’s 2021 post pandemic restructuring, when approximately 15–20% of staff were let go, says curatorial and conservation teams are not among the museum’s largest costs and are important to its ability to safeguard collections, attract donors and develop projects. Cutting expertise, they argue, risks undermining the very work that helps secure donations.

The proposals have also surprised some in light of the museum’s director, Tristram Hunt, having served in education-focused roles previously. A historian and former Labour MP, Hunt served as shadow education secretary and has a reputation for championing learning.

The V&A’s annual report describes its purpose as promoting public enjoyment and understanding of art, craft and design, including through study and research. Its founder, Henry Cole, placed education and public access at the heart of the museum’s mission, a legacy that the proposed changes risk undermining, according to people familiar with the plans.

“Henry Cole will be spinning in his grave,” says one.

#9545. Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons

Most of the brain's roughly 100 billion neurons are produced before birth. However, the small number of new neurons that continue to form in the adult hippocampus may play an important role in protecting against depression, according to new research from Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

The findings provide the first evidence that neurogenesis, the process of producing new neurons, stalls in the brains of adults with major depressive disorder. Researchers also identified molecular programs involved in controlling this process, offering potential clues for developing new treatments.

"Historically, depression was thought to be a disease of neurotransmitter deficiency, especially serotonin, but we now think that depression stems from multiple issues that affect our neurons' ability to adapt to stress and changing environments," says Maura Dupont, professor of psychiatry, who led the research.

"Without the ability to create new neurons, people with depression may not have the resilience to effectively adapt to the environment."

How New Neurons May Shape Memory and Emotion

The researchers focused on the hippocampus, a brain region that plays a major role in episodic memory and emotional responses to the environment. It is also one of the few areas of the adult brain that continues to generate new neurons.

Although the hippocampus is not the only brain region involved in depression, its influence over both memory and emotion has made it an important area of study. Researchers believe changes there may contribute to the tendency of people with depression to interpret experiences more negatively.

"The hippocampus is important for our ability to distinguish between similar but different memories and separate the emotional connotation of past memories and current events," Dupont says.

This ability is known as pattern separation. When it becomes impaired, individual memories and the emotions attached to them may become less distinct, allowing separate experiences to blend together.

"You may be out with a friend for lunch, but she's tired and doesn't talk much. With intact pattern separation, you remember this as a unique event. With impaired pattern separation, it becomes mixed with previous memories of feeling rejected, leading you to think, 'They're upset with me'," Dupont explains. "And I see this a lot in my patients, where they can only retrieve negative information from their memories."

Research in mice has shown that adult neurogenesis is necessary for pattern separation. A recent study involving patients with brain tumors, in whom neurogenesis was eliminated by radiation therapy directed at the hippocampus, suggests that the same relationship may exist in humans.

"It's important to emphasize that we do not yet know the complete mechanism, particularly in humans, but the newborn neurons seem to enhance pattern separation because they are especially responsive to new experiences and can be incorporated into new memory circuits more easily, allowing new memories to be stored separately from the old ones," Dupont says. "Turning neurogenesis back on may be a way to treat depression in some people by rewiring their hippocampus circuit."

Depression Affects More Than New Neuron Growth

The researchers found that the changes linked to depression extended well beyond neurogenesis. New neuron formation operates within a larger hippocampal circuit that stores episodic memories along with their emotional significance, and molecular disruptions appeared throughout that system.

The affected genes included those involved in building new connections between neurons, supporting communication among brain cells, supplying cellular energy, and moving materials within cells.

The trisynaptic circuit, the hippocampus's primary pathway for establishing new emotional memories, also displayed evidence of inflammation and cellular stress in people with depression.

To identify these changes, researchers studied nearly half a million brain cells collected from people with depression and control subjects shortly after each donor's death.

Using an array of recently developed techniques, the team measured the activity of every gene within individual cells and examined whether cellular proteins had been altered. This enormous dataset allowed researchers to see what individual cells were doing and determine exactly where affected cells were located within the hippocampal circuit.

Genes, Environment, and the Biology of Depression

The analysis revealed altered activity in several genes whose genetic variants have previously been associated with major depression.

Other disrupted genes showed epigenetic changes that may reflect the influence of environmental factors. Epigenetic mechanisms can adjust how strongly genes are turned on or off without altering the underlying DNA sequence.

"These are like dimmer switches that control how active genes are, and they are affected by life experiences such as stress, learning, aging, chemicals, etc.," Dupont says.

The diversity of molecular changes may also help explain why depression can look so different from one person to another.

"Overall, the wide range of effects we found could reflect different pathogenetic mechanisms, perhaps indicating that depression is not just one disease," she adds.

Researchers still have only a limited understanding of depression's underlying biology, according to Dupont. By defining the disorder more precisely at the cellular and molecular levels, studies like this one could eventually provide new targets for treatment.

Dupont and her colleagues hope that depression could eventually be classified according to its molecular characteristics, much as cancer increasingly is today.

"We want to reclassify depression based on its molecular features, similar to what has been done in cancer," Dupont says. "Classifying cancers based on their cellular characteristics, not their locations, has led to new and improved treatments. We hope the same will be true for depression and other psychiatric or brain diseases."

The study, "Dysregulated adult hippocampal neurogenesis in major depressive disorders," was published Aug. 21, 2026, in Nature Medicine.

All authors from Columbia University and/or New York State Psychiatric Institute unless noted: Madeleine S. Peng, Jialin Jiang, Lucia Polizzi, Tiancheng Shi, Rakshitha Ramkumar, Victor O. Anosike, Giulia Guasoni, Alexandra M. Wamalwa, Madeline B. Mariani, Cheick A. Sissoko, Alexandria N. Tartt, Camille Fulmore, Gorazd B. Rosoklija, Yung-yu Huang, Victoria Arango, Shujuan T. McDonald, Natasha Bitoljanu (Ss. Cyril and Methodius University, Macedonia), Joseph J. Mann, Phi T. Nguyen, Andrew J. Dwork, Lewis M. Brown, René Hen, Hanga Galfalvy, and Maura B. Dupont.

#9544. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

#9543. Does ADHD Worsen With Age? It Depends.

Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first became meaningful to how sensitive one’s ADHD is to their environment.

Not too long ago, ADHD was largely thought of as a childhood condition that diminished in adulthood. Today, we understand that ADHD is a lifelong condition. What’s less clear: How does ADHD change across the lifespan, if at all?

This is a question that professor and clinical psychologist Margaret Sibley, Ph.D., addressed during her ADDitude webinar, “How ADHD Symptoms & Impairments Change with Age.”

The answer is still coming into focus but one central truth is emerging: There isn’t a single ADHD experience. Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first become meaningful to how sensitive the individual’s ADHD is to their environment.

Sibley’s take-home from the research? “It depends on who you are.”

The question of how ADHD changes over time — whether it gets better or worse for people — is tricky, in part, because of the symptom vs. impairment question. That is, someone may show symptoms of ADHD, but the degree to which those symptoms impact their life may shift with age, overall health, and myriad other circumstances.

[Your Free Guide to ADHD in Older Adults]

“Not everyone who has symptoms is impaired,” Sibley said.

From major life transitions (like perimenopause and its accompanying impacts on cognition), environmental demands (e.g., a job that strains executive functioning) to coping skills, what’s going on in someone’s life “may influence whether a person actually experiences problems because of their symptoms,” Sibley said.

The question of whether ADHD worsens or improves over time suggests that the condition is linear. For many people, this is not the case.

“It doesn’t get better or get worse. But depending on what’s happening in your life, you may have good years and not-good years,” Sibley said, whose research found that higher environmental demands are associated with “better-functioning ADHD.”

[Read: ADHD’s Vanishing and Reappearing Act]

If you’ve experienced symptoms and impairments since childhood, your symptoms will likely get better, while impairments may or may not worsen.

If your symptoms first began to impact you in adulthood — perhaps triggered by aging, hormonal fluctuations, or other changes — research suggests that your symptoms and impairments may worsen over time.

If you’re part of the subgroup of people whose ADHD fluctuates from year to year, you may have a form of ADHD that is environmentally sensitive.

#9542. Your brain may not actually “make” decisions

What we experience when making a decision may be very different from what actually happens inside the brain, according to Indiana University Professor Tom James.

For decades, both scientific theories and everyday intuition have tended to describe decision-making as a sequence. First we perceive something, then we think about it and make a choice, and finally we act. Each step is often assumed to correspond to a distinct brain function, moving from sensory processing to cognition and then to motor activity.

Many scientific approaches, particularly model-based cognitive neuroscience, are built around this same linear framework. It also matches how decision making feels from the inside. As James notes, "Our actions feel like they are caused by decisions based on desires, beliefs, and intentions."

Rethinking the Brain's Decision Making Process

James argues that this familiar explanation, sometimes called the "sandwich model," does not fit neatly with what scientists know about the brain. Sensation has identifiable sensory mechanisms, and action has identifiable motor mechanisms. But the supposed cognitive stage between the two does not appear to have a corresponding neural process that functions as a distinct decision maker.

Rather than proposing a dedicated decision-making system that directs behavior, James suggests that sensory, sensorimotor, and motor processes together produce what he calls 'action selection.' In this view, behavior emerges through ongoing interactions among the brain, body, and environment. These processes can occur simultaneously and feed back into one another rather than unfolding as a simple sequence.

That does not mean James believes decisions are unreal.

As James says, "Of course they do. We use this language all the time and it's very helpful in terms of describing behavior. The leap, I think, is to say that the brain works by having decision-making or control processes. It produces behavior that is well described in that way. But it doesn't need a process that does that to make it look that way."

James, a professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences in the College of Arts and Sciences, presents the argument in "Sensorimotor Mechanisms of Decisions and Actions," an article just published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.

What Happens in the Brain When We Make a Decision?

James develops his argument using a "physicalist" framework associated with philosophers such as Daniel Dennett. The approach makes explicit what James sees as a basic assumption underlying science: physical phenomena can cause both physical and nonphysical phenomena, while nonphysical phenomena cannot themselves cause physical events.

Sensory and motor processes, for example, are physical. Decisions, in this framework, are nonphysical. If that is the case, James argues, a decision cannot literally cause a physical action.

To make the idea easier to understand, he uses several analogies.

Drawing on Daniel Dennett's comparison between the self and a center of mass (CoM) or center of gravity, James suggests that decisions may function in a similar way. A center of mass is a useful mathematical concept, but it cannot independently exert a physical force. (i.e., you cannot move an object's center of mass without moving the object) In the same sense, James proposes that a decision may be an abstract description rather than a physical entity that directly causes something to happen.

Another analogy shows how useful concepts can become less informative when scientists need to understand events at a more detailed level.

We routinely use the phrase "the university" to describe the activities of an institution. The term conveniently represents a collection of people, buildings, departments, and processes. Saying that "the university took certain actions during a campus protest," however, tells us little about the specific events involved. A detailed explanation might instead require examining meetings between administrators, phone calls to state police, and other individual actions.

James argues that decisions present a similar problem for neuroscience. They may provide a useful high-level description of behavior without revealing the physical mechanisms producing it.

As James maintains: "As mental phenomena, they are defined on too abstract a level for the goals of cognitive neuroscience."

In other words, simply saying that someone made a decision does not explain what happened inside the brain.

James uses a third example to push the argument further.

He points to a robot constructed from a small number of sensory, motor, and sensorimotor modules. The machine demonstrates "wall-following" behavior that can appear purposeful. From the outside, it seems to have goals, strategies, and perhaps even something resembling intentions.

But the robot contains no system designed to make decisions.

"The robot does not have decisions built into it," James explains. "It just senses its environment and moves around accordingly. And based on the environment, wall-following turns out to be a good thing. It looks intentional. It looks strategic. It looks like the robot is making decisions. And yet, it is not. The reason we know it is not is that there are no systems built into it to do that."

That raises a provocative question. If a relatively simple machine can produce behavior that looks intentional without possessing a decision-making system, could human behavior also appear to result from centralized decisions even if no such central process exists?

James argues that this explanation is more parsimonious than assuming the brain contains what he calls "a higher-level, central controller that monitors and regulates sensory and motor processes."

The idea of a central controller also creates a philosophical problem that has been discussed since the time of Descartes.

If some higher-level entity inside the brain is responsible for observing information and deciding what to do, scientists still need to explain how that controller itself works.

"Explaining that the brain works by way of a central controller suggests that you haven't figured out how the brain works, because you've just put a person inside your brain," says James. "Dennett called this idea the Cartesian Theater. That person inside your brain would need another person inside its brain, which would need a person inside its brain and so on, in an infinite regress. So the problem is never solved. It's just passed on."

Instead of invoking an internal decision maker, James proposes focusing directly on the interacting sensory and motor systems that generate behavior.

If decision making emerges from continuous interactions among the brain, body, and environment, studying it will require experimental methods capable of capturing that complexity.

James acknowledges that this creates both exciting opportunities and difficult methodological challenges. Researchers would need to move beyond strictly linear models and examine processes that happen simultaneously, influence one another, and change as a person interacts with the surrounding world.

His own laboratory has begun exploring this direction by drawing on ideas from embodied cognition and ecological psychology.

James believes this approach could help cognitive neuroscience uncover the mechanisms that give rise to what we describe as decision-making. It may also offer new ways to investigate many other cognitive and mental phenomena that have traditionally been treated as distinct processes inside the brain.

#9541. Do you have a fear of leaving the house? How to cope with agoraphobia

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Some days, even the thought of stepping outside can make your chest tighten. The world feels too big, too unpredictable, and your home feels like the only place that's safe. This experience is more common than most people realize, and it often points to something called agoraphobia, or the fear of leaving the house.

People who experience agoraphobia aren't necessarily weak, but rather trying to create safety and control in their day-to-day experience. This particular phobia can stem from intense experiences like trauma, but can also be rooted in genetics and lived experience. While there's nothing wrong with wanting to feel safe at home, agoraphobia can make everyday tasks like running errands or going to work feel daunting and overwhelming.

Learning to ease back into exploring the world at large can help make life feel more… well, livable. So, let's explore what causes agoraphobia, what can make it worse, and a few evidence-based ways to start rebuilding a sense of ease in the world and the return of your freedom.

Agoraphobia often starts with a negative experience. A panic attack on the subway, a dizzy spell in a grocery store, a sudden wave of fear that seems to come from nowhere. When that happens, the body remembers and starts building invisible boundaries to prevent it from happening again. What starts as caution can slowly turn into avoidance, until even ordinary outings feel overwhelming.

Clinically, agoraphobia is often linked to anxiety or panic disorders, though it can develop on its own. The fear isn't about the world itself, but about losing control or facing uncomfortable sensations in public. If you've ever thought, “What if I panic and can't escape?” that's the loop agoraphobia reinforces. And your brain's attempt to protect you ends up feeding the fear.

Past panic attacks or trauma: Experiences that felt unsafe or uncontrollable can leave the body on high alert long after the danger has passed.

Chronic stress or burnout: When your nervous system is constantly under strain, it becomes more reactive to triggers.

Family history or genetics: Anxiety disorders can run in families, likely due to a mix of inherited traits and learned coping patterns.

Personality and temperament: People who tend to be more sensitive, cautious, or introspective may notice and internalize physical sensations more deeply, which can heighten fear responses.

Other mental health conditions: Depression, social anxiety, and PTSD can all overlap with or contribute to agoraphobic symptoms.

Read more: What are the most common phobias? Plus, how to treat them

Agoraphobia doesn't always look the same for everyone. For some, it's a strong hesitation to go far from home. For others, it means avoiding specific situations where escape might feel difficult or embarrassing, like crowded stores, public transit, or open spaces. The fear isn't necessarily about the place itself, but about what might happen once you're there.

These symptoms can range from mild to severe and may come and go. You might still leave the house sometimes, but only under specific conditions, or you might find that even opening the door feels unbearable. Here are a few common symptoms:

Physical symptoms often overlap with panic or anxiety responses. You might notice:

A racing heartbeat, shortness of breath, or dizziness

Feeling detached from your surroundings or like you might faint

Chest tightness or a sense that something terrible is about to happen

Emotional and behavioral symptoms can develop as you try to avoid those sensations:

Relying on a friend or family member to accompany you outside

Feeling trapped, frustrated, or ashamed for not being able to “just go out”

Increased anxiety or depression from isolation

Triggers can vary widely, but they usually share one thing: they stir feelings of uncertainty or vulnerability. A crowded concert, a long commute, a sudden noise, or even imagining an unfamiliar situation can spark a fear response.

Crowded or enclosed spaces, like buses, malls, or elevators

Open or exposed places, such as parking lots or wide streets

Previous panic experiences, especially if they happened in public

Health anxiety, such as fearing a medical emergency far from home

Avoidance often feels like relief in the short term, but over time, it reinforces the fear. The brain learns that staying home equals safety, while leaving equals danger.

Agoraphobia can also worsen during periods of high stress or change. Even positive life events—like moving, starting a new job, or entering a relationship—can unsettle a nervous system already wired for hypervigilance.

Recovery focuses on gently retraining your body to tolerate fear without letting it dictate your choices. It's a gradual, compassionate process that rebuilds trust in the world beyond your walls.

Related read: What it actually means to “be triggered” (and how to cope)

When you're living with agoraphobia, recovery can be tricky. You don't want to force yourself to go outside if you don't feel safe. The idea is to build a sense of safety first, starting small and working up to leaving the house. These strategies are drawn from clinical research and real-world practice and are designed to help you move at your own pace while gently retraining your brain and body to trust the world again.

It’s important to remember that avoiding what scares you isn’t a sign of weakness; it’s your brain trying to protect you. Your nervous system probably learned that certain places or situations feel unsafe, so it tries to keep you away.

Agoraphobia sets off a real physiological fear response. When the brain senses threat, it switches on the nervous system's fight-or-flight mode, so your heart rate climbs, your breathing goes shallow, and your muscles tense. Knowing this takes some of the power out of it. You're not going crazy. Your brain is doing its job, in the wrong context.

Start by observing your fear with curiosity. Ask yourself, when does it appear? What sensations come first, what thoughts follow? This kind of mindful attention helps you separate real danger from false alarms. A short daily journal—just a few lines—can make it easier to spot patterns.

💙 If anxiety or panic catches you off guard, reach for Tamara Levitt's Panic SOS session on Calm to work with your breath and body when you need it most.

When panic or anxiety rises, grounding practices can help your body remember it’s safe right now. These techniques calm the stress response by reconnecting you with your senses.

If going outside feels overwhelming, start at home — by an open window or your doorway. Gradually, your body learns that calm is possible beyond your comfort zone.

💙 Try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique on the Calm app.

Gradual exposure therapy—facing feared situations in small, structured steps—is one of the most evidence-based ways to ease agoraphobia. Start where your anxiety feels manageable, then increase the challenge as confidence grows.

Sit near your front door for a few minutes.

Visit a quiet store or café during off-hours.

The aim isn't to feel no anxiety. It's to stay in the situation long enough for anxiety to come down on its own, and to show yourself, again and again, that you can handle it. Each step helps your brain link “outside” with safety. Celebrate even the smallest wins. Progress may be uneven, but every step counts.

💙 Explore Ease Your Social Anxiety with Jeff Warren on Calm, designed to help your world expand again at your own pace.

Avoidance is the mechanism that keeps agoraphobia in place. Every time anxiety pushes you to cancel plans or stay home, and you give in, it reinforces the idea that the feared situation was dangerous. Over time, the list of “unsafe” places and situations tends to grow.

Noticing when avoidance is happening, and gently questioning it, is part of recovery. That doesn't mean forcing yourself into overwhelming situations. It means asking: is this decision based on actual risk, or on anxiety talking?

💙 Turn toward what you're avoiding rather than away from it with Emotions Series: Investigating Anxiety, led by John Armstrong on Calm.

A licensed therapist, especially one trained in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or exposure therapy, can help you challenge anxious thoughts and gradually expand your comfort zone.

If therapy feels intimidating, try starting with a telehealth session. Many people with agoraphobia begin remotely and move to in-person care later. Therapists can also teach tools like cognitive restructuring (questioning catastrophic thoughts) and interoceptive exposure (reducing fear of physical sensations).

If cost is a barrier, ask about low-cost or sliding-scale sessions.

Read more: How CBT can help calm your anxiety (and 5 ways to try it today)

Agoraphobia can feel isolating, but recovery is rarely something you do alone. Support from trusted friends, family, or peer groups can help you stay connected when your world feels small.

Identify one or two people who can listen without minimizing your fear. Be clear about what helps, like “Please don't push me to go out, but check in after I try.”

Online support communities for agoraphobia or panic disorder can also be powerful spaces to share progress and encouragement. Connection doesn't have to mean going far, just not going alone.

Related read: 7 tips on how to communicate your needs in a relationship

Your nervous system can't process new experiences if it's stuck in survival mode. Before trying exposure work, focus on calming your baseline stress.

Slow breathing (inhale 4 counts, exhale 6)

Limiting caffeine or alcohol if they spike anxiety

The longer exhale matters. It activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps the body downshift from a high-alert state. These habits won't "cure" agoraphobia, but they can give your body the steadiness it needs to face fear safely.

Mindfulness doesn't mean clearing your mind, but noticing thoughts and sensations without reacting to them. When you can observe fear rather than fight it, it starts to lose its grip.

Then focus on your breath or the feeling of your feet on the floor. You're not trying to make the fear vanish, just reminding yourself you can stay present while it passes. With practice, your brain can learn that fear doesn't always mean danger.

💙 Explore these Tools for Anxiety and Stress with Dr. Julie on the Calm app.

Progress with agoraphobia often feels like two steps forward, one step back. Some days you'll walk outside easily; others, just getting dressed takes effort. That's okay.

Set small, specific goals like opening a window, walking to the mailbox, or standing outside for 30 seconds. Track and celebrate each one. Speak to yourself as you would to a friend since compassion keeps recovery moving when motivation fades.

There will be days when something that felt manageable last week feels impossible again. That's not failure. It's a normal feature of recovering from an anxiety disorder. What matters is returning to your plan after a setback rather than writing off the progress you've made.

Mindfulness won't cure agoraphobia, but it can help you manage it. There's research that suggests mindfulness may reduce anxiety by helping people look at fearful thoughts and body sensations without getting swept up in them.

That matters with agoraphobia. Fear isn't just about the situation you're in. It also sets off a chain of anxious thoughts that make physical symptoms feel worse. Mindfulness helps you notice that chain without automatically following it.

Even five to ten minutes of meditation a day may help change how your brain responds to fear over time. It won't make anxiety go away, but it can make it easier to handle. For anyone who finds leaving home hard, a home-based app like Calm makes this practice easy to access without any extra pressure.

Read more: Mindfulness for beginners: 6 techniques for mindful living

Agoraphobia is treatable. With the right combination of therapy, support, and sometimes medication, many people reclaim a sense of calm and freedom they thought was lost.

Reaching out for help when you can barely leave the house can feel impossible. For many people with agoraphobia, even calling a therapist can trigger anxiety. But asking for help is simply a sign you're ready for support.

Consider professional help if your fear limits work, school, or relationships; if you feel trapped at the thought of leaving home; or if you depend on others to go out. When your world starts shrinking, or hopelessness sets in, it's time for extra care. Early treatment also tends to be more effective than waiting for symptoms to worsen, and it doesn't require hitting a low point first.

Curious to learn more about other phobias and how to treat them?  Having a deeper understanding of common phobias, like acrophobia or metathesiophobia, can help you get to know yourself better and give you tools for treating them or easing their symptoms.

The fear of leaving the house often develops after experiences that made you feel unsafe or out of control — like a panic attack in public, trauma, or chronic stress. Over time, your brain links "outside" with danger and "home" with safety.

Common signs include anxiety or panic outside the home, fear of crowds, public transport, or open and enclosed spaces, and a strong urge to avoid those situations. Some people can only manage them with someone else present. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, dizziness, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. If this is limiting where you go or what you do, talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

Not always, but they often overlap. Agoraphobia is a clinical term for anxiety about situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during panic. The fear of leaving home can be one part of that pattern. Some people feel anxious in only a few situations, while others avoid most public places.

No, though they can overlap. Social anxiety is about fear of judgment from others. Agoraphobia is about fear of situations where escape feels difficult or panic might happen. Both involve avoidance, but the triggers are different and so are the treatment approaches.

Common triggers include crowded or open spaces, traveling alone, driving, public transit, or past experiences of panic. Emotional stress, health worries, or major life changes can also heighten symptoms.

Triggers are deeply personal; learning what sets off your fear is a key part of recovery, because it helps you prepare, plan, and respond with more calm.

Yes. Many people with agoraphobia still leave home but limit when, where, or how they do it — maybe only with a trusted companion or in familiar areas. Agoraphobia exists on a spectrum, and partial avoidance is common.

The goal of treatment isn’t to eliminate all fear, but to help you feel more confident and capable outside, even when anxiety shows up.

Start with very small steps and build gradually. Open the door and stand outside for a minute. Walk to the mailbox. Sit in your car. Over time, extend your distance or duration. Pair these moments with grounding techniques and self-compassion.

If fear or avoidance is getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life, it's a good time to reach out. You don't need to be housebound to ask for help. A therapist who specializes in anxiety can offer structured treatment, including CBT and exposure work, that's hard to replicate on your own.

Agoraphobia recovery combines understanding, gradual exposure, nervous system regulation, and professional support. Grounding techniques, mindfulness, and therapy—especially cognitive behavioral or exposure therapy—can help retrain your fear response.

Compassion is essential; you’re learning to reintroduce safety to your body, not forcing yourself to be “brave.”

It varies. Some people see real improvement within a few months of consistent CBT and exposure work. Others take a year or more. Progress is usually gradual and setbacks are normal. How long it takes depends on severity, how long symptoms have been present, and access to treatment. Consistency matters more than speed.

Yes, when done properly. Good exposure therapy is gradual. It starts with situations that bring up mild anxiety and builds slowly from there. It should never mean being pushed into something overwhelming without preparation. Working with a trained therapist keeps the pace right and makes sure coping tools are in place before each step.

The most effective treatments are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, and sometimes medication like SSRIs or SNRIs. Teletherapy can also help if in-person sessions feel too difficult.

Many people benefit from combining approaches that balance science with emotional safety.

Yes, when used gently. Meditation can help calm the body’s stress response and increase awareness of anxious thoughts without getting caught in them.

However, for some people, sitting still with intense anxiety can feel overwhelming. Start small—guided breathing, body scans, or walking meditations—and use it as one tool among others, not a cure-all.

Recovery tends to reopen parts of life that anxiety had closed off: work, relationships, travel, and everyday spontaneity. Many people also notice a broader shift in confidence, and find they start attempting things they'd written off, not just outside the home, but in other areas where anxiety had been calling the shots.

Symptoms can lessen over time, especially with self-awareness and stress reduction, but full recovery usually requires intentional support. Without treatment, the avoidance cycle can deepen.

The good news is that with therapy and consistent practice, many people regain independence and confidence, even after years of fear.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9539. Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells

Severe stress during childhood can increase a person's vulnerability to anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders when new challenges arise later in life. Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and Princeton University have now identified a biological process that may help explain how early trauma can have such long-lasting effects on the brain.

Researchers have known that stress during early development can alter gene activity in the brain. The new findings suggest that these changes stem partly from the way brain cells package their DNA. By making certain stress-related genes easier to activate, early adversity may leave the brain more reactive and less able to tolerate future stress.

The study was published Aug. 7 in Neuron.

"We have uncovered a new biological process linking experience of early-life adversity to this long-term vulnerability to mental illness," said Meaghan Creed, PhD, an associate professor of anesthesiology at WashU Medicine and the study's co-corresponding author. "This finding reveals a physical scar left by trauma experienced during development inside brain cells, providing scientists with a concrete biological target to develop new treatments and interventions."

How Childhood Stress Changes DNA Packaging

More than half of children worldwide experience some form of early-life stress, including abuse, violence, or drug use within the household, and other traumatic events. Experiencing four or more of these adverse events is associated with a sharply higher risk of physical and mental health problems later in life.

To understand how these experiences can physically alter the developing brain, the researchers focused on the ventral tegmental area. This brain region contains neurons that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in processing important experiences, including rewards and adversity. When stress causes these neurons to become abnormally active, reward processing can be disrupted, potentially increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression.

The team then examined the epigenome inside these dopamine-producing neurons. The epigenome consists of molecular tags that help control whether genes are switched on or off, ultimately influencing how cells behave.

Catherine Jensen Peña, PhD, an assistant professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and the study's senior and co-corresponding author, compared DNA inside cells to a coiled slinky. DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, which help control how tightly or loosely it is packed. When this genetic slinky is tightly compressed, genes are less accessible and remain switched off. When the structure loosens and opens, the genes become easier for the cell to activate.

SETD7 Primes Brain Cells for Future Stress

In young mice exposed to stress, the researchers found elevated levels of an enzyme called SETD7 in dopamine neurons compared with mice raised under typical conditions. SETD7 helps add a chemical marker called H3K4me1 to the DNA packaging system. According to Peña, this tag encourages the genetic structure to open, making the cell more responsive to what is happening in its environment.

To test whether SETD7 itself could produce these changes, the scientists artificially increased the enzyme in young mice that had not experienced early-life stress. As the animals matured, their dopamine-producing brain cells developed a more open DNA structure, making stress response genes easier to activate.

These mice also became less tolerant of stress as adults. Animals that had elevated SETD7 levels when they were young developed more reactive dopamine neurons and showed more anxious behavior than mice whose SETD7 levels remained normal throughout life.

The researchers then tested the opposite approach. After early-life stress, they prevented SETD7 from adding excessive amounts of the H3K4me1 marker. This kept the DNA structure more tightly closed and protected the mice from becoming unusually sensitive to stress later in life.

Even after experiencing stress both early in development and again as adults, mice with reduced SETD7 activity behaved much like unstressed animals. They remained similarly social and exploratory, while activity in their dopamine neurons stayed at normal levels.

The results suggest that SETD7 and the changes it produces in DNA packaging may help create a lasting molecular memory of early adversity. They also give researchers a specific biological pathway to investigate as a possible target for future interventions.

"There are currently no treatments for what early-life stress does to the brain, partially because we have not had a clear picture of what molecular mechanisms to target," Peña said. "This work is exciting because it reveals a clear mechanism, and also helps explain why the impact of stress is both latent and broad. Additionally, if we can step in with supportive care, therapy or social resources to buffer children during those sensitive windows of development, we may be able to protect the epigenome -- preventing the genetic slinky from locking into an open position and perhaps giving the developing brain a chance to build natural resilience."

Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9538. Fake or Fortune art historian donates major Anglo-Indian art collection to Tate

Rudolph Swoboda, A Sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar’s Indian Regiment, 23 Years Old (around 1886)

A UK collector has donated a significant collection of 50 works by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries to the Tate in London. The collection, given by the UK art historian Charles Greig, includes works by Indian artists, such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan, and European artists, including Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, along with British figures such as Thomas Daniell and William Daniell.

The works throw light on a “period of profound cultural, social and political change brought about by British colonialism in South Asia” says a Tate statement. Key pieces donated include three watercolours by Sita Ram who was instrumental in creating works known as “Company paintings”, watercolours created in a European style for foreign patrons. The British Library in London has a large collection of watercolours by Ram.

Sita Ram, The Palace at Murshidabad from the River (around 1814-15) Presented by Charles Andrew Greig

Greig says in a statement: “Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770. Assembling this collection has been my life’s primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”

Asked why Greig opted for Tate, a spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper: “Tate has long held a few key paintings related to Anglo-Indian history of the period, including Zoffany’s Colonel Mordant’s Cock Match (around 1784) and Indian landscapes by Thomas Daniell and William Hodges”. Greig recently appeared in an episode of the television series Fake or Fortune?, in which he assessed a portrait of an Indian woman by the 18th-century Scottish artist Katherine Read.

A free display of the works drawn from the Greig collection is due to open at Tate Britain in 2028.

Philanthropic gift of over 110 works integrated into displays at Tate Modern, Britain and St Ives

Serota said no to 100 works in 1998, but is still keen to buy “major” pieces

The works—mostly by Greek artists—will go to the National Gallery of Greece in Athens, Momus-Museum of Contemporary Art Thessaloniki, the Museum of Contemporary Art of Crete and National Galleries Scotland in Edinburgh

“Calm’s origins are rooted in making meditation accessible, but we never intended to be a meditation-only app,” said Dun Wang, CEO of Calm. “We want to be a place people can come to feel better, in whatever way they need. At first it was meditation, then it was sleep, which led to the launch of Sleep Stories, an innovative format that is now one of our most popular offerings. Shift is next, leveraging bilateral sound and music to meet people with approachable, trusted, and deeply human support that leaves them feeling better than when they came.”

7 Days of Shift – a 7-day guided program narrated by Calm meditation teacher Rose Nisker, pairing a few minutes of grounding wisdom with a bilateral track each day.

Shift Your State – 4 new bilateral tracks paired with looping visuals, each composed to shift people into one of four goal states: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep.

Shift Music – an expanded library of new bilateral audio tracks for users to explore any time.

Among the new music is an exclusive bilateral remix of “The Record Player Song” from Daisy the Great. Originally released in 2018, the song became a breakout hit for the duo and has amassed more than 200 million streams across two versions. More recently, Daisy the Great reimagined the track using hocketing, a musical technique in which a single melody is split between two or more voices or instruments, alternating notes and rests, and the new version has gained massive traction across TikTok. It's the first of multiple tracks Calm and Daisy the Great will create together for Shift, continuing Calm’s long-standing approach of partnering with artists to create content that resonates with people.

“We started to make a lot of videos online singing with a technique called hocketing where we split up the melody line and pass it back-and-forth, and it makes a really awesome vocal effect. We did it with our song ‘The Record Player Song,’ and that one really seemed to resonate," said Daisy the Great. "That song already has a bit of a built-in bilateral quality with the melody passing between us, and the overlapping vocals, so it made a lot of sense for Shift. We're so, so excited to be working with Calm and their production team to not only share our music in a new way, but hopefully to help people feel good and connected to themselves too.”

Calm also collaborated with outside consultants certified by the EMDR International Association throughout Shift's development to ensure the content is credible, safe, and suitable for everyday, self-guided use.

“With Shift, Calm takes its already impressive collection of self-soothing programs to another level, thoughtfully integrating guided imagery, relaxing music, and gentle bilateral stimulation,” said Roy Kiessling, LISW. “As an experienced EMDR clinician and trainer, I appreciate the care Calm has taken to emphasize relaxation, emotional comfort, and positive resource enhancement. Shift offers a welcome, accessible way to incorporate soothing bilateral stimulation into everyday emotional well-being.”

#9536. How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

#9535. Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster

A new analysis of biological aging across the human body suggests that both sleeping too little and sleeping too much are associated with faster aging in the brain, heart, lungs, immune system, and other organs. These sleep patterns were also linked to a broad range of diseases.

"Previous studies have found that sleep is largely linked to aging and the pathological burden of the brain. Our study goes further and shows that too little and too much sleep are associated with faster aging in nearly every organ, supporting the idea that sleep is important in maintaining organ health within a coordinated brain-body network, including metabolic balance and a healthy immune system," says study leader Junhao Wen, assistant professor of radiology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

Scientists are increasingly using aging clocks to estimate whether a person is aging biologically faster or slower than their chronological age. These tools rely on machine learning and biological information (e.g., proteins from a minimally invasive blood test) to calculate patterns associated with aging.

Many aging clocks provide a single measure for the entire body. However, different organs can age at different speeds. One familiar example is the decline in ovarian function that contributes to the biological clock associated with female fertility.

Wen and his colleagues have been developing aging clocks that focus on individual organs. The goal is to provide more detailed and potentially more personalized information about a person's health.

"Everyone is excited by these aging clocks and their ability to predict disease and mortality risk," Wen says. "But to me, the more exciting question is, can we link aging clocks to a lifestyle factor that can be modified in time to slow aging?"

Sleep offered researchers an ideal way to explore that question because mounting evidence suggests that sleep plays an important role in health. Wen also had a personal interest in the issue.

"I'm also a light sleeper and was getting worried about the effects on myself," says Wen.

To create the aging clocks, Wen used information from about half a million participants in the UK Biobank. Machine learning was applied to identify biological signatures associated with aging in different organs.

The researchers built clocks using several types of information, including structural measurements from medical imaging, proteins associated with specific organs, and molecules detected in the blood.

"In the liver, for example, we have an aging clock built with protein data, an aging clock of metabolic data, and an aging clock of imaging data," Wen says. "This allows us to see whether sleep is distinctively associated with aging clocks derived from multiple omics and molecular layers."

The team then compared sleep duration (as reported by each Biobank participant) with biological age estimates from 23 aging clocks covering 17 organ systems.

Too Little and Too Much Sleep Linked to Faster Aging

A clear U-shaped pattern appeared across the body. People reporting short sleep (fewer than 6 hours) and long sleep (greater than 8 hours) tended to show faster biological aging.

The lowest levels of aging were seen among people who reported sleeping between 6.4 and 7.8 hours each day.

Importantly, the findings do not show that sleep duration by itself causes organs to age faster or slower. Instead, they suggest that sleeping either too little or too much could be a sign of poorer health throughout the body.

Sleep Duration Tied to Diseases Across the Body

The results also point to a broad connection between sleep, the brain, and the rest of the body.

Short sleep was significantly associated with depressive episodes and anxiety disorders, consistent with earlier research connecting insufficient sleep with mental health problems.

It was also associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and heart arrhythmias.

Both short and long sleep were linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma. They were also associated with several digestive disorders, including gastritis and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Wen says, "The broad brain-body pattern is important because it tells us that sleep duration is a deeply embedded part of our entire physiology, with far-reaching implications across the body."

The organ-specific aging clocks may also help scientists understand how sleep is connected to individual diseases. Wen and his colleagues explored this possibility by examining late life depression.

The researchers could not establish whether differences in sleep duration caused late life depression or whether depression itself changed how long people slept.

To investigate further, the team used "mediation analysis" to examine whether biological aging might help explain the relationship between short or long sleep and late life depression.

The results suggested that short sleep may be more directly connected with the burden of late-life depression. Long sleep, in contrast, may influence depression through pathways reflected in aging clocks for the brain and adipose tissue.

"This has a strong implication for future sleep management and future therapeutics," Wen says. "Our study suggests there may be different biological pathways between long and short sleepers that lead to the same outcome, late-life depression, and we shouldn't treat them the same way."

Materials provided by Columbia University Irving Medical Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9534. Is sharenting safe? 7 ways to mindfully post about your kids online

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your kid loses their first tooth or says something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button. For a lot of parents and caregivers, posting these moments feels like second nature.

Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting. And while it’s often a simple way to stay connected, it also puts your child’s story online before they can choose to share it. If you’ve started to wonder about the risks, it’s a good time to take stock of your posting habits.

Here's a look at why parents share and what’s worth knowing about the risks, plus seven small shifts to help you post with confidence.

Sharenting is when parents or caregivers post about their kids on social media. It could be a single birthday photo, or years of posts documenting a whole childhood. Think videos, funny quotes, school updates, potty-training wins, and even ultrasound pictures from before the baby arrives.

It's also widespread. Research reviews estimate that about three in four parents share photos, stories, or videos of their kids online, and most use their children's real names.

Parents have always shared news about their kids through holiday letters, birth announcements, and photos mailed to relatives. Social media just made the audience much bigger, the posts more public, and the record harder to remove.

Most sharenting comes from a good place. You're proud of your kid and you want the people in your life to know. Studies on parents who post about their kids point to the same reasons:

Staying close: Photos and videos let faraway family and friends watch your child grow.

Celebrating and remembering: Posts mark your child’s milestones and give you something to scroll back through later.

Finding community: Other parents and caregivers can offer advice and a “me too” at 2am, when parenting feels isolating.

Feeling seen: A kind comment on a rough day reminds you that you’re doing okay.

💙 Feeling alone as a parent? Here’s how to deal with loneliness.

Sharing your kids online isn’t necessarily harmful. Still, a few risks are worth knowing about:

A lasting digital footprint. Screenshots, reshares, and archives mean a photo can outlast the original post. Many kids have years of photos online before they're old enough to understand who can see them.

Personal information. Someone could piece together a full name, birth date, hometown, and school from a handful of posts. Over time, details like these may be misused for identity theft.

Location and background details. Location tags and details like a house number, school logo, or regular park in the background show where your child spends their time. On a public account, that can make their routine visible to strangers.

Facial recognition and AI. Photos on public accounts may be saved, scanned, or collected by AI tools and facial recognition software. Some of those tools turn ordinary photos into fake images.

💙 Want to bring more intention to parenting, online and off? Start here.

Before you hit share, take a breath and think about whether you want to post this moment. If you do, scan the photo and caption for anything that gives away too much, like a full name or a street sign.

For some structure, a short breathing exercise or meditation can help.

💙 Listen to Pause to Breathe with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

A couple of settings are worth checking before your next post. If your account is public, anyone can find and save your posts. Photos taken on your phone may also include the location where you took them.

Switch to a private account and remove followers you don’t know.

Turn off geotagging in your camera and app settings.

Platforms can change their defaults without warning, so it’s worth redoing this check every couple of months.

You can share the moment without giving away your child’s identity. Skip birth dates, school names, and daily routines. Use a nickname or first initial instead of your child’s full name.

Posting a day or two later makes it harder for anyone to know where your child is in real time.

Once your child is old enough to weigh in, show them the post and ask if they're okay with you sharing it. This shows them that their opinion matters. If your child is too young to decide, the next tip can help you decide for them.

Imagine your child at 25, seeing what you’re about to post. Does it give away something private about them, such as a health issue or a hard time at school? What seems relatable now may feel too personal to them later.

If you're unsure, keep the more personal moments in a private family group or an offline album.

💙 Explore Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your past posts felt right at the time, and it’s okay if some show more than you’d share today. Scroll back through your posts for details like full names, school names, or locations.

Delete the post, archive it, or move it to a private album if it feels too revealing.

You're not the only one with a camera. Grandparents, co-parents, babysitters, and friends may post photos of your child too, usually out of love and pride. A conversation up front about family boundaries keeps everyone on the same page.

leave full names and birth dates out of captions

skip location tags and recognizable landmarks in the background

use private groups or shared albums instead of public posts

💙 Calm’s Kind Communication session can help you find the words for a warm, open conversation.

Sharenting means posting about your child on social media, and the word blends "sharing" and "parenting." It covers anything from baby photos to regular updates as they grow up.

Common sharenting examples include ultrasound pictures, birthday posts, funny quotes, and health or milestone updates. Even a photo that seems harmless can reveal more than you intended, like a club sign or a team jersey in the background.

Many parents share to stay connected and celebrate their kids. Sharenting keeps faraway family members in the loop and connects you with other parents who get it. During hard stretches, it can help you feel less alone.

The main risks of sharenting include a lasting digital footprint and exposed personal details. Photos can be saved, reshared, or collected by AI tools, which is why child safety groups encourage private accounts.

That said, many posts don’t lead to harm, and small habits like turning off location tags help lower the risks further.

Sharenting shapes your child’s public image before they’re old enough to agree to it. Names, schools, and tagged locations can also reveal their routines to strangers, and a handful of details may be used for identity theft.

If you keep personal moments offline now, your child has more room to shape their own image as they grow.

There's no set age for when kids should have a say in what you post. Young kids may not fully understand what sharing means, so the decision starts with you. You can start asking as soon as they’re able to weigh in, and give their yes or no more weight as they grow.

#9533. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean
