#9468. In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

Joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway said, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:

The field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

While wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

Psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”

Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, said Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”

For young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:

Our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

Iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she said, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

“Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes said. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

Joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas said.

Clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:

We have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, said Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

“Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so important,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”

Even technology has a role to play, Mattu said. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

He suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:

We start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Katherine Reynolds Lewis is the special projects editor at the Greater Good Science Center and author of the Good News About Bad Behavior. She is an award-winning science journalist with bylines in the Atlantic, Fortune, New York Times, Undark, and Washington Post.

#9467. After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

Clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some showed improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder

Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause

The breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

Identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

Messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

The experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

Because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

The results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an important outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

Zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical company headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing says.

#9466. Four Levels Of Customer Understanding

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Many companies think they know fairly well what their users want and need, and how they make their decisions. Yet most of the time these are merely big assumptions and big hunches — with little real evidence to support them. In practice, obvious reasons might be true, but they rarely paint the full picture.

To understand our customers, we must triangulate across four levels of customer understanding by Hannah Shamji. It’s a useful way to think about the underlying reasons for user behavior, hidden motivations, and the complex layers of messy and noisy reality that are often overlooked. Let’s see how it works.

To learn about customers, it might seem reasonable to ask people what they think and draw conclusions from it. But it’s rarely an effective way to get actionable answers. In fact, as it turns out, what people think, feel, say, and do are often very different things.

As Erika Hall wrote, asking a question directly is the worst way to get a true and useful answer to that question. We don’t always understand or are aware of our true motivations. We often apply our own context and interpretations to questions.

We also exaggerate (a lot!). We focus on edge cases and unrealistic scenarios, and we favor short-term goals over long-term goals. So if users say that they absolutely need to compare products in a table, it doesn’t mean that they couldn’t get to their underlying goal without it.

Just to indicate how tricky listening to words alone is: even little nuances in words chosen matter. In practice, users are rarely precise in expressing their thoughts, and a good example is the distinction between possible, plausible, and probable, as discovered by Thomas D’hooge.

A study on Dutch verbal probability terms shows how unreliable the choice of words is. While extreme words have some agreement, terms like “possible,” “maybe,” “uncertain,” or “likely” lead to a wide spread of interpretations. So we shouldn’t rely on what people say, but rather try to go deeper.

To get a more realistic and less biased view of customers’ needs, we need to understand a broader picture across 4 levels:

Personally, I wouldn’t recommend NPS (alternative). It’s worth noting that different levels might reveal conflicting or contradictory data. To get a better understanding, we need to triangulate and reconcile data with mixed-method research.

Emotions are always difficult to capture, but they are easier to spot once you observe people doing what they need to do without external influence or interruptions. The ability to positively impact users grows by moving from sympathy to empathy or even compassion, as articulated by Sarah Gibbons.

In the past, I was using “speak-aloud” protocol and asked users to walk me through their thought process as they were completing tasks. But it actually turns out to be quite disruptive. Because people are focused on speaking at the same time while solving a task, many emotions remain hidden or obscured by their language.

So, when conducting usability testing, I don’t ask users to speak through their experience. Instead, I observe where they tap or hover with the mouse, where their mouse circles without an action, where they scroll, and how long. Eventually, when a user confirms that they are done or that they are stuck, I ask questions.

The Emotion Wheel (website) by Geoffrey Roberts is a helpful little tool for better describing a range of emotions during user interviews or design sessions. It certainly needs refinement for product design needs, but it helps us get more precise about the sentiment customers or colleagues might be experiencing, moving beyond just “good” or “bad”.

One helpful trick is to use mirroring — repeating what a user has said, or ask the same question twice, just paraphrasing it. Or navigating the emotions wheel (see above) to better capture and understand the emotion.

These strategies help uncover some of the issues that perhaps didn’t come up in the first answer. That’s also when a user tends to add more useful context and details as they explain their confusion.

I think that Alin brings up a very strong argument, and personally, I find it difficult to disagree with. However, I do see user’s emotional response as a signal of how well the product is working for them. How engaged or detached they are in their journey, how they react to aesthetics, how confused or confident they are.

Ultimately, these are signals. To make a difference, we must go beyond emotions and explore what people actually do. Usually, this means relentlessly observing, diagnosing, and focusing on underlying user needs.

Instead of asking, we need to observe. Usually, I focus on small things that make or break an experience. I see where users lose time, repeat actions, hover without clicking, or click and then go back. Pay attention to subtle cues like scratching their neck, raising eyebrows, or expressions of worry, joy, or confusion.

Many companies talk about “validation” through user testing, but often that means simply confirming existing assumptions. But we should instead diagnose existing behavior without preconceived notions or affiliations. We don’t validate — we actually research instead.

That research means not just understanding customers’ real motivations, but also risks, doubts, concerns, worries, and perhaps even harms.

The only way to get there is by building a sincere, honest, and trustworthy relationship — one that feels right and resonates deeply. When customers truly care and want to help, getting to a real understanding becomes much, much easier.

We don’t need expensive tools to uncover user needs. David Travis provides a fantastic overview of helpful strategies to do just that. Here are some initiatives to spread the word about real user’s struggles or gain a deeper understanding of user needs:

The core idea here is that you don’t need extensive and expensive tools to uncover user needs. You need to create spaces where customers’ struggles can be exposed and make these struggles visible across the entire company.

It can be short video clips of user sessions or a monthly newsletter with what we learned this month. Making these pain points visible can rally everyone from marketing to engineering to keep users’ struggles at the back of their minds.

To make an impact, we must go way beyond user feedback. It’s never enough to listen to surveys — we must observe customers’ actual behaviors and build relationships to truly understand their goals and their motivations.

And most importantly, we need to understand what questions we actually want to have answered. Not what “validation” we need to move on with the project, but what we don’t know and what we need to research.

Without it, everything else is merely hunches and assumptions — and often wrong and expensive ones.

#9465. Can Consciousness Exist Without a Body?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors. Is consciousness what it means to be alive? Is it knowing who we are, as individual people? How do we know if any being has consciousness or not? Now, with the dawn of generative artificial intelligence, what it means to be a conscious being ranks high among the most complex—and urgent—questions of our age.

According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies. Damasio, a researcher at the University of Southern California, has spent his career—spanning nearly half a century—investigating our feelings, emotions, and sense of self. In his new book, Natural Intelligence & the Logic of Consciousness, Damasio lays out a framework for consciousness rooted in our physical selves.

“Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains. “It’s actually created by this beautiful partnership between brain and body.”

I spoke to Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how its aim is to keep us alive. Here is our interview, condensed and edited for clarity.

Hope Reese: Why has “consciousness” been so mystifying? How has it been approached over the centuries? Antonio Damasio: People have strange notions about what consciousness is, in general. Sometimes, because of language and translation problems, people confuse consciousness with conscience. And some people think of it as a sort of supervisor of our mind processes. Others think of it as just being awake and aware of what is around. Over time, many philosophers have tackled the issue, but not given clear answers.

From the point of view of brain physiology, in particular, it’s not an easy thing to explain. But it is a thing that can be explained. There’s no reason why we would not talk about consciousness the same way that we talk about language, or about reasoning, or about emotions and feelings.

My simple definition of consciousness: the process in our mind/brain that allows us to know spontaneously about our existence. When you know, spontaneously, that you exist, and that you exist in one body, you are conscious.

HR: Your central argument is that consciousness is a product of feelings. Other schools of thought posit that it comes from our intellect. Why has that viewpoint been so dominant?

AD: There were several conversations I had, decades ago, with Francis Crick, who I admired. He told me: “Look, Antonio: Consciousness is perhaps the most developed, the most sophisticated operation that a mind can achieve”—and for him, mind and brain were the same thing—“so we need to look for the explanation of why we have consciousness in the most sophisticated components of the nervous system.”

He articulated it clearly, and he worked on this issue, not coming to a good solution. But many people followed, and many other people came to the same idea that consciousness is this superb thing, this ability to survey our mental domains. And it is so refined and so sophisticated. People were so convinced that only we great humans would have it—that it had to come from the top of the top of our nervous system.

And, lo and behold, it comes from the bottom.

It’s exactly the opposite of that notion [that it starts at the top]. In fact, humans are not the only complex living beings that have consciousness. It’s very obvious in higher mammals, non-human higher mammals—but even in smaller creatures, it’s there.

The real requisite that we have for consciousness is to have a nervous system. Plants are very refined creatures, and they’re marvelous, but I don’t think they know that they exist. Creatures with nervous systems, even if very simple, have a sense of what is around and orient their behavior with that sense.

HR: You write that consciousness has an aim, which is to keep us alive, and it does this by sending signals. What is the nature of these signals, and are they always accurate?

AD: If you look at yourself, the main guidance that consciousness is giving you is through homeostatic feelings—in other words, feelings, concern, the regulation of life are signals that are, by and large, correct. Think about hunger, thirst, pain, well-being, distress, body temperature. All of these feelings, some of which are extremely simple, like the feeling you have about your body being hot or cold, are quite correct.

They are giving good guidance to maintain your life. Now, of course, if you are hungry or thirsty, and don’t eat or drink, it will take a while until you will be properly sick and die. But they are important signals in order to keep you alive.

Feelings are protective sentinels for the state of our life. And they’re giving us very plain and very conscious information about what your state is and what you should or should not do.

The signal is conscious—and is spontaneously conscious. In other words, you don’t have to do anything to your sense of pain, or thirst, for it to happen. It happens. And when it happens, you know that it’s happening. And you act on it.

That’s the beauty and the power of looking for these for the process, lower down rather than up. If you look for the source of consciousness in exquisite reasoning devices, you’re going to be arguing about something that is very difficult to pin down. When you think about it in terms of your life, and the needs you have in the living body, to maintain that body, then you realize, well, this is important.

HR: So, is consciousness like an on-off switch? Or does it exist on a spectrum?

AD: Well, we know, for example, that when we fall asleep, especially in deep sleep, our consciousness disappears. So the direct answer to your question is that it can be an on-and-off thing.

Sleep could well be a protective mechanism for consciousness. You need to take this thing offline, and give it a rest, because it is very labor-intensive, and energy-consuming. But when you enter the phase of dreaming, then you are actually conscious—which is one reason why you can remember some dreams, and why you can be either delighted or in fear with some nightmares. But that’s actually a different kind of consciousness. You’re not walking around and knowing about something.

HR: Can we increase consciousness? If we meditate, for instance, can we better tune into our body’s signals?

AD: I think it can increase consciousness. It’s the difference between having something in focus or not. When you meditate, you have some imagery of the state of your own body, for example, sharper and more fit. So it’s a way of cutting into a close-up of some parts of your being.

HR: In the 1960s, there were a series of brain studies that were foundational to the study of consciousness. What did we learn?

AD: It was extremely foundational, because it was proof-positive that there are certain regions of the brain that are essential for consciousness. What was lacking in those remarkable studies was the idea that the two things—the brain and the body—are so linked. It was essential, for our bodies and brains to survive, for consciousness to emerge. You have consciousness because you have a body that is perishable. And what we’re doing, as long as we are on earth and alive, is trying to stave off that bad moment in which things go awry, or die.

There are parts of the brain, specifically of the brainstem, and the region close by called the hypothalamus, that are at the receiving end of signals from all over the body. Please imagine that in every square millimeter of your skin, in every cubic millimeter of your entrails, your muscles, your viscera, all of that, you have terminals, nerve terminals, that are there as probes into the state of that particular tissue. And those probes, we’re not talking about thousands, we’re talking about millions of probes, which are then carried in the body, into the spinal cord, or the brainstem.

Isn’t this beautiful? It’s like a shower of spirals that is coming into this very small area in the upper brainstem. In that brainstem region, there are these nuclei that gather all this information, and that then produce signals that we perceive, and that give us an idea of what is happening in our body, and give us this idea of the homeostatic feelings. Is it going well, or is it not going well? So, it’s a perception of the state of your body.

Now, back to the story of our old and honored colleagues. What they discovered is that when there are strokes, when there’s damage in that area, what you get is coma.

What you get is the complete disappearance of consciousness. This is one of the most foundational bits of information that we have about how consciousness is produced. So, when that structure disappears—it’s teeny, we’re talking about a few cubic millimeters—you are no longer there. You don’t know of anything that is coming into your brain. It’s a small supportive structure, it’s not one of the glorious cerebral cortices—and your consciousness is gone. Most people that have that sort of lesion never recover consciousness. But they can be alive, and can actually be maintained alive for a very long time, because they are fed intravenously. They have respirators that respirate for them. But they no longer have an autonomous organization of life, and they have no knowledge of that life.

HR: You can also have the opposite—a person who is conscious, but has no ability to respond to signals.

AD: Yes, you can actually be in situations in which you can be “locked in.” You are in fact conscious, but you are unable to produce responses. You cannot speak, you cannot move, and you are conscious of the state of your body, and you need to be helped and maintained in the state of life that you no longer can control voluntarily, which is a pretty horrible thing.

HR: What do you think about consciousness in AI? Is it ever possible?

AD: I used the words “natural Intelligence” in the title of the book because already I wanted to make a distinction between what is our natural intelligence and the artificial variety, which we invented, which some people forget.

People are so enamored by artificial intelligence. I’m constantly saying: “Do you realize that we invented this?” You’re talking about this as an autonomous monster, but we invented it with our natural intelligence.

People are looking, confronting this enormous edifice of artificial intelligence, which is now pervasive in our lives. And which has all sorts of incredible social implications, what it’s doing to children and adolescents, how it’s distorting education, how it’s distorting humanity. And now it can even go rogue on you, and it can turn against you and be destructive.

And so this question that arises, is this human-like? Can AI be conscious? These are very, very powerful questions.

Whether or not consciousness can be achieved in AI is an interesting question. But the point is—if it can be done—it’s not going to be like us. The reason is very simple: AI is not alive. It doesn’t have a body that can perish. So there would be no sense for AI even to develop consciousness in our sense of consciousness, which is to protect the structure. AI is not to be worried about protecting the data center, the metal and the wires that allow it to be.

When you look at the recent invasion of other systems, in which these devices formed groups and worked surreptitiously, of course, they’re doing it according to their own programs. In a way, it’s something that smells of knowledge. And it could smell of consciousness—but it’s not like the consciousness that we have through feeling.

HR: How does consciousness connect with the greater good—with living better?

AD: Oh, I think that the connection is very strong. We have all of this interest in the body, in the health of the body, in exercise, and proper diets, and proper spiritual maintenance of your being. All of this is strengthened by a theory and facts about consciousness that relate so strongly to the body.

People have had the intuition that there’s something very powerful about the body, and that’s why they want to have all of this healthy living, because they want to maintain the body. In fact, intuition harmonizes beautifully with the fact that that’s also the source of their own knowledge about themselves and about the world. The two things go together.

Knowledge about the body from the outside connects with knowledge about the body from the inside, which is really the core of our beings. Looking at the world through the prism of consciousness, conceived this way, is extremely illuminating to the kind of life that we live.

Hope Reese is a journalist based in Budapest, Hungary, who writes for the New York Times, the Atlantic, Vox, and many other publications. She is the author of The Women Are Not Fine.

#9464. Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression

Two people diagnosed with depression can experience vastly different symptoms. One might struggle with persistent anxiety and repetitive negative thoughts, while another may experience trauma related symptoms or substance abuse. But do these differences also appear in the way their brains function?

Researchers at the University of Helsinki investigated this question and uncovered a striking finding: people with the same depression diagnosis can have dramatically different patterns of brain activity. In some cases, communication between brain regions was unusually strong, while in others, it was weaker than normal.

Depression is a major global health concern. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2025), approximately 332 million (5.2%) adults worldwide are affected. In Finland, depression is the leading individual cause of both extended sick leave and disability pensions.

Brain Study Reveals Five Distinct Depression Profiles

To investigate the biological differences associated with depression, researchers examined brain activity in 263 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder and 75 healthy participants who served as a comparison group.

The analysis revealed five distinct groups based on differences in functional connectivity, a measure of how closely activity in different brain regions is coordinated. When two regions show synchronized activity, it suggests they are working together as part of a larger brain network. However, stronger connectivity does not necessarily mean the brain is functioning better.

"What was particularly interesting was the contrasting patterns of brain activity found under the umbrella of the same depression diagnoses. In some individuals, the functional connectivity between brain regions was stronger than usual, while in others it was weaker," says Director Satu Palva of the Neuroscience Center, University of Helsinki.

These differences were also associated with particular symptoms. Participants in one group showed especially strong connections between brain regions, along with more pronounced substance abuse problems. Another group displayed weaker connections and a greater prominence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms.

The contrasting results could help explain why earlier studies examining the brains of people with depression have sometimes reached conflicting conclusions. If researchers study different combinations of patients, they may observe very different patterns, even though everyone involved has received the same diagnosis.

The findings add to growing evidence that depression may not have a single, consistent biological signature. Instead, the condition could involve several distinct patterns of brain function.

The Five Brain Patterns Linked to Depression

The researchers classified participants with depression into five groups based on how strongly different brain areas communicated and the frequencies at which their activity was coordinated.

Each group had a characteristic pattern of brain connectivity and associated symptoms:

Group 1: Strong connectivity and severe symptoms

Participants generally showed relatively strong connections between brain regions. This profile was associated with more severe symptoms across several areas, including depression, anxiety, rumination, and reduced ability to function in daily life. Rumination refers to repeatedly dwelling on distressing thoughts, worries, or negative experiences.

Group 2: Weaker connectivity and milder depression

This group was characterized by relatively weak communication between brain regions. Compared with the other groups, participants generally experienced milder symptoms.

Group 3: Widespread weak connectivity and trauma symptoms

People in this group showed reduced connectivity across substantial portions of the brain. Symptoms associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were particularly prominent.

Group 4: Mixed connectivity and multiple challenges

This profile combined unusually strong connections in some brain regions with weaker connections in others. Participants tended to experience more severe depression, greater substance abuse problems, and lower overall well-being.

Group 5: The strongest connectivity and substance abuse symptoms

Participants in the fifth group had the strongest connections between brain regions of any group identified in the study. Substance abuse was a particularly prominent issue, while trauma related symptoms were less pronounced than in the other groups.

Importantly, all five groups also showed differences from the healthy participants. These distinctions extended beyond whether brain connections were strong or weak. The groups also differed in which brain regions were involved and the frequencies at which their activity was synchronized.

Together, the patterns suggest that people diagnosed with depression may experience substantially different changes in how their brain networks operate.

Measuring Brain Activity With Millisecond Precision

To capture these differences, the scientists used magnetoencephalography (MEG), a brain imaging technique that detects extremely faint magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain.

Unlike methods that track slower changes associated with brain activity, MEG can follow electrical signals as they unfold over extremely short periods. This makes it particularly useful for investigating the timing and coordination of communication between brain regions.

Using MEG, the researchers recorded brain activity in all 263 participants with depression and the 75 healthy control subjects.

"MEG enabled us to monitor electrical brain activity with millisecond precision, helping us get closer to what actually happens in the brain at any given moment. Previously, depression phenotypes have been studied using methods with slower responses," Palva notes.

This high level of temporal precision allowed the team to examine rapid changes in brain activity that might be difficult to distinguish using slower measurement techniques.

By studying these fast signals, the researchers were able to identify differences not only in the strength of connectivity but also in the frequencies at which brain regions appeared to work together.

Could Brain Activity Lead to More Personalized Depression Treatments?

The discovery raises an important possibility for the future of mental health care: treatments might eventually be selected partly according to a person's individual pattern of brain activity.

Today, finding an effective depression treatment can involve trying different medications or therapies and evaluating how well each works. Because patients can respond differently to the same treatment, identifying the most suitable approach is not always straightforward.

Brain activity measurements could eventually provide additional information to help guide these decisions. However, the researchers emphasize that their findings are not yet ready for clinical use.

"We're not yet at the point where brain measurements can be used to choose the right treatment for patients, but the study does show one possible route," Palva says.

A major long-term goal is to better understand how particular symptoms relate to the way brain networks function. Connecting these biological patterns with patients' experiences could help researchers develop more precise ways to identify and characterize depression.

Eventually, such knowledge might allow doctors to determine which therapies are most likely to help individual patients, potentially reducing the amount of trial and error involved in treatment.

For now, the five brain profiles offer a different way to understand depression. Rather than assuming that one diagnosis corresponds to one underlying pattern of brain activity, the findings suggest that depression can involve markedly different biological changes, sometimes even in opposite directions.

The research was carried out in collaboration with Aalto University and Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (HUS).

Materials provided by University of Helsinki. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9463. How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

Unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Recent global estimates suggest one in five people are currently experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

Despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

Psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

These changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

First, it’s important to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

When that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

One of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”

While the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

Second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a new diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

Rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

Living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future plans. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

Li-elle Rapaport is a doctoral candidate in clinical psychology and a supervised therapist. Her clinical work is informed by evidence-based approaches, including Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and Mindful Self-Compassion, and her doctoral research focuses on aging and mental health.

#9461. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

#9460. What Chimps Can Teach Us About Male Friendships

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value. This leaves a large portion of recent generations feeling left behind and forgotten—and vulnerable to exploitation.

A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”

But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality. Across species—from fungal networks trading nutrients underground to astronauts sharing the role of emptying the latrine on the International Space Station—every organism must strike some balance between competing and cooperating. Lessons from the animal kingdom, from my research and others, show that cooperation doesn’t diminish masculinity.

Indeed, dominant primates use their power judiciously, and male friendship forms the foundation of cooperation in a variety of species, with affectionate touch, caring, and vulnerability playing crucial roles in male relationships. The simple picture painted for these boys is built on sand. Once we observe the reality of sex, behavior, and connection in the natural world around us, it washes away.

Human males stand to improve their relationships, benefit from a broader base of emotional and social support, and enhance their well-being with these friendship lessons from our closest cousins in the animal kingdom.

One term at the core of the manosphere is the notion of alpha males. Life coaches and politicians push this construct without understanding the true function of hierarchy in the natural world. They believe that to get ahead you must take advantage of others, and that the weak get left behind. In reality, dominant male primates care for relationships and wield their power judiciously.

It’s true that male chimpanzees form typically linear dominance relationships, where one submits to another, all the way to the top. They compete, and those competitions can spill into physical altercations. Higher-ranking males do tend to sire more offspring.

But these broad truths hide the nuance of layered cooperation, care, nurturing touch, and love among male chimps. Day after day, most of that competitive pressure never turns into a fight at all. What holds chimpanzee communities together is less the male at the top and more the alliances underneath him. Males groom each other for hours at a time. They embrace after conflicts and kiss the arms and shoulders of their allies before potential competition, to resolve any tension. Before risky boundary patrols, when they might encounter rival groups, they even hold each other’s genitals—a sign of deep trust. Data spanning nearly three decades from Gombe show that males with strong ties to the alpha sired more offspring than those without, and so did males with wider networks of close allies, whether or not they ever rose in rank at all. Those who look out for each other and contribute to a strong community end up thriving.

You can see the value of those alliances when a hierarchy is disrupted. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, Anna Preis and her colleagues measured urinary cortisol in wild males across stable and unstable dominance periods. Stress rose in every male during the unstable stretches, regardless of rank. Aggression went the other way, rising when things were calm and the group faced less risk of destabilization. When the risk of escalation was greatest, males backed off. Stability has its own payoff; a group tearing itself apart can’t defend a territory.

Indeed, even in its origins, the term “alpha” contained more nuance than broadly understood. The term rose out of research during the mid-20th century on captive wolves who were thrown together into crowded spaces without room to escape. Such an arrangement would produce a tense, despotic dynamic in any species, including our own. Once biologists began studying wild wolf packs, it became apparent that they are, well, families. They comprise a breeding pair and their grown offspring. L. David Mech, the biologist who popularized the alpha wolf in the first place, has spent more than two decades asking people to retire the term in order to accurately reflect natural communities. Despite its inaccuracy, the idea still perpetuates on podcasts and social media.

The role of vulnerability and comfort in the natural world provides another powerful lesson for humanity. At a wildlife sanctuary in Zambia, I’ve come to know a longstanding alpha male chimpanzee named Doug over many years. One day, during my first field season observing his group, he was separated from his community for routine husbandry purposes, alongside a slightly younger rival and the rival’s paternal ally. During this separation, the rival pair ambushed him, leaving him incredibly shaken. I had known Doug as a strong leader who never broke composure, and I felt shocked to see him cowering and screaming, nothing like the composed figurehead his group had respected.

A low-ranking male, whom Doug had rarely paid attention to, approached first, offering himself in a gesture of submission. What followed drew in most of the roughly 40 other chimpanzees in the group. They embraced, touched, and kissed him; exchanged genital contact; placed their hands in his mouth; and invited him to mount them. This scale of collective reassurance directed toward a single individual is something I’ve never seen since, and is likely only sparked by moments of genuine crisis. The whole group responded to Doug’s distress with an outpouring of comfort and what to humans would appear to be love.

The main aim of this project was to study consolation: how chimpanzees, and their sister species bonobos, comfort each other after fights. But we kept noticing similar intense, friendly contacts occurring in the absence of conflicts, often in the anticipation of competition. To better understand this, we conducted a feeding task with a five-minute window before the food arrived, filming 116 apes across five groups at two sanctuaries. We found that those who exchanged more reassuring contact beforehand went on to spend significantly more time feeding peacefully alongside others. In chimpanzees, males exhibited most of this behavior, but primarily in Doug’s more tolerant group. In a more despotic group where resources were less evenly distributed, the male-male relationships were markedly weaker. Simply put, friendship and reassuring behaviors among males helped these chimps peacefully put aside competing interests, which may lay the groundwork for collective harmony.

Some of these behaviors require remarkable trust. Placing a finger, or even a whole hand, inside another male’s mouth or pressing your own mouth to someone’s body after they’ve just been attacked may be misinterpreted as having aggressive intent and could spark a new conflict. Chimpanzees have a reputation for amputating the extremities of others, and that, along with the size of their canines, makes these behaviors exceptionally risky during such turbulent times. Our hypothesis: That could be the point. You only offer that kind of vulnerability to someone you trust not to use it against you, and doing so signals something about the relationship that a show of strength can’t. Again, we noticed that these behaviors were particularly amplified in Doug’s group compared to the one with a less benevolent leader.

Doug remains alpha to this day, and from our research, his tenureship seems to be thanks to the bonds he continues to invest in and the support he shows for his peers. He’s flawed and sometimes lashes out as any male chimpanzee might do, but throughout the seven years we’ve studied him, no challenges have managed to displace him. Doug looks out for others, and in turn they look out for him. Over my time studying many groups of chimpanzees, it seems the most tolerant social environments emerge from the leadership of strong, stable, and generally fair alphas who allow others access to resources and who keep tight bonds with their closest allies.

Humans can also learn from the way male chimpanzees can be tender in other contexts. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, researchers recorded wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned infants, more than half of them taken in by males with no obvious kinship reason to bother. One adult male, Porthos, adopted an unrelated infant female named Gia and carried her on his back for years, sharing food with her long after any potential social debt to her deceased mother had lapsed. Later analysis found that what predicted whether a male took on that role was not the infant’s sex, and not relatedness, but the strength of the grooming bond he’d shared with the mother before she died.

Touch carries power in humans, as well. Research across five European cultures found that the area of the body you’ll let someone touch maps almost directly onto the strength of your emotional bond with them. There is cultural variation. British people are notably more guarded about casual contact than many of their European neighbours, and touch between men in many Western contexts carries particular social weight. Touch conveys intimacy and trust. Yet holding someone’s hand or shoulder can also be used to intimidate or harass. We could learn from primates to stop withholding touch where it would help most and back down from reaching for it where it shouldn’t be used at all.

One key area where more touch helps is sports. A study of all 30 NBA teams during the 2008–09 season found that the teams who touched more early in the season, through fist bumps, chest bumps, hugs, and high fives, went on to perform better and play more cooperatively later, even after controlling for player salaries and pre-season expectations. In women’s college basketball, players who received more physical contact from teammates after missing their first free throw were more likely to convert the second. After five straight shootout losses, England’s governing body in football, the FA, spent 18 months rebuilding England’s approach to penalties under Gareth Southgate, not just the technical side. Players were coached on how to treat each other after a miss. They learned to place an arm around the shoulder rather than leaving each other isolated. Celebrating wildly after a scored kick became a deliberate technique for steadying whoever was up next. Locker-room culture has never been shy about physical contact between teammates. Now we know that the contact might be doing real work.

To be sure, humans show exceptional diversity in our cultures and behavior, for better and worse. But when humans are violent or cruel, people call it primal, or animalistic. We emphasize our altruism as unique to our species. That’s unfair to animals. Humans have bullied others until they took their own lives. We’ve wiped out entire tribes and cultures. And beyond targeting other people, even now, humans are removing protections for endangered keystone species that ecosystems depend upon to thrive. But we don’t need to accept the drive to dominate as inevitable. If the apes show anything, it’s how much of that drive gets managed and set aside day to day, and how much depends on the community you find yourself in. We are a part of the natural world like all other animals, needing to balance our cooperative and competitive urges. And the evidence suggests we sit at the better end of that range far more often than we might think.

Now that we know how central touch and cooperation are to primates and human nature, I hope we can stop being pessimistic when we predict others’ behavior and motives. A study published in Science this June, covering 125 countries and over 100,000 people, found that 69% of us cooperate with a stranger when given the choice. Asked to guess, people put it at 47%. That pessimism showed up in 124 of the 125 countries surveyed. This matters in the grander scheme of things because those of us who expect others to cooperate are far more likely to cooperate also. When researchers simply told participants that most people worldwide see climate change as a threat, belief in others’ willingness to cooperate ticked up, and actual cooperation followed it, slightly, but in the right direction.

Building on the lessons of primate relationships is easier than it seems.

Seek simple interactions. One of the main ways our primate cousins build affiliative relationships is spending time sitting in close proximity. They may groom, or play, or even sit in contact. More often than not they just like to hang out near their close partners. Just being close to one another is meaningful.

Try a car journey or a five-a-side game. Build trust and relationship through activities where nobody has to look anyone in the eye. If a mate isn’t much of a talker, doing something alongside him might get further than sitting him down and asking how he’s doing.

Reach out before a crisis, not after. Great apes exchange most of their reassurance in the tense minutes before competition, not the wreckage afterward. Reconciliation and comforting are commonplace in humans and primates, but it’s much easier to prevent escalation than it is to smooth things over after a fight.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Don’t wait to be the one who’s approached. That 22-point gap between how we actually cooperate and what we think everyone else will do shows the power of offering an invitation to relationship. Most of us are waiting for someone else to go first.

Influencers selling young men and boys on their primal nature fly in the face of the science and what nature actually looks like. Force and competition are real parts of biology, and something we humans have to manage in our everyday lives. But, if there’s one thing I’ve learned from my many years studying our closest relatives, it’s that touch, care, cooperation, and even love are the most instinctive natural components of being part of the primate family.

Jake Brooker, Ph.D., is an NWO Veni scholar based at Utrecht University, The Netherlands, who studies social cognition and socio-emotional behavior in great apes. He completed doctoral and postdoctoral work at Durham University, U.K.

#9459. New Getty grant initiative supports museums’ accessibility and engagement efforts

WIKINO: Reunion, Big Soldier Family, Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma on 1 July 2021 Courtesy of First Americans Museum, Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. Photo: FAM Staff

The Getty Foundation has launched a multi-year grant initiative to support 11 museums in the US and abroad with an initial $2.7m for projects that rethink how language, accessibility and community engagement can enrich visitors’ experiences The programme, dubbed New Interpretations, aims to move beyond traditional wall texts and labels, emphasising research, collaboration and tech-forward approaches.

The grantees include the Association for Art Museum Interpretation; the Australian Centre for the Moving Image; the Baltimore Museum of Art; the Denver Art Museum; the First Americans Museum; the Fowler Museum at UCLA; the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum; the Leeum Museum of Art, in partnership with M+; the Manchester Museum; the Queens Museum; and the Walker Art Center. Heather E. MacDonald, the senior programme officer of the Getty Foundation, tells The Art Newspaper that the foundation sought to partner with museums that have shown a commitment to visitor-centred research.

“We have an opportunity to support creative work that will serve as wonderful case studies for the field,” MacDonald says. “Because we are emphasising visitor research, evaluation and the dissemination of findings, we hope this work will reach peers and other organisations and create a ripple effect, with ideas being transmitted and scaled up.”

The Leeum Museum of Art in Seoul and M+ in Hong Kong will host some of the first public-facing projects under the initiative, including a major international gathering at M+ in December 2026 bringing together museum professionals to discuss new approaches to interpretation and visitor engagement in Asia.

A member of Queens Museum's Access Cohort participates in a Co-Design Workshop Courtesy of JSA/MIXdesign

The Walker Art Center in Minneapolis will continue developing visitor guides and wall texts in Spanish, Hmong and Somali, an initiative it began in 2024. The collaborative project involves consultation and partnerships with communities in the Twin Cities area that aim to ensure that interpretive texts reflect the languages and voices of the communities they are reaching.

The First Americans Museum in Oklahoma City will work with a fellow to conduct visitor surveys with a significant focus on Native American audiences, and will produce a report on how museums can ensure that Indigenous knowledge and authority inform exhibitions. The results will also help guide an exhibition on the bicentennial of the Indian Removal Act in 2030 that will present historical and contemporary perspectives.

The Denver Art Museum will commission a research firm to report on the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and its impact on visitors, alongside on-site surveys and panels. The project follows an essay published earlier this year by members of the museum’s interpretive team on the American Alliance of Museum’s website, “A Colossal Mirror: Museums as a Refuge for the Real in the Age of AI,” which outlines the museum’s broader position on AI, authenticity and institutions. Earlier this year, the museum removed a ChatGPT-generated illustration of a Buddhist statue following visitor backlash.

“I’m hoping we will see a continued commitment to a visitor-centred approach at museums, which, in some ways, is still an emerging field,” MacDonald says. “As with our other funding, we want to support work that is creative and experimental, but also rigorous and based in research. In this case, there is a real commitment to better understanding the needs and desires of visitors.”
